name: WASP Wildfire Protection Full Kit
pick: Best gutter-mount kit
priceNote: Kit pricing varies by number of heads and hose length
summary: Canadian-designed gutter-clip sprinkler heads that install in minutes without tools and run off a standard garden hose. The full kit covers a typical roofline and includes hoses and splitters.
pros: No-tool gutter clip install
Made in Canada, widely stocked by Canadian retailers
Runs off garden hose pressure
cons: Depends on municipal pressure unless paired with a pump
Coverage limited on steep or multi-level roofs
bestFor: Homeowners who want a same-day DIY sprinkler defense.

guide.howItWorks: Plastic sprinkler heads clip over the lip of your eavestrough and throw a low arc of water back across the roof deck and down the wall. The point is not to soak the shingles — it is to keep the roof, the fascia and the first metre of wall wet enough that an arriving ember goes out instead of taking hold, and to raise humidity in the air immediately around the house. You run it for the hours either side of a fire front passing, then shut it off.
guide.market: Gutter-mount ember-defense kits are a small market with maybe a dozen serious players, most of them Canadian and most founded after the 2016 Fort McMurray fire. They cluster into three tiers. At the bottom, generic tripod and impact sprinklers repurposed from irrigation — cheap, no roof coverage. In the middle, clip-on kits like WASP, Platypus and Flash: purpose-built heads, garden-hose fed, $600–$2,500 depending on head count. At the top, permanently plumbed systems like Frontline with dedicated pumps, tanks and remote activation, at $15,000–$40,000 installed. WASP sits squarely in the middle tier and competes mostly on being tool-free and Canadian-stocked rather than on throw distance or build quality, where Platypus arguably edges it.

features.label: Gutter-clip mounting
features.detail: Heads hook over a standard 5 in K-style eavestrough. No drilling, no roof penetration, no ladder work beyond reaching the gutter line.

features.label: Garden-hose supply
features.detail: Standard 3/4 in GHT fittings. Kit includes splitters and hose so the whole roofline runs off one or two outdoor taps.

features.label: Modular head count
features.detail: Kits are sold by head count — typically 4, 6, 8 or 12 — so you scale to roofline length rather than buying a fixed package.

features.label: Low-pressure operation
features.detail: Designed to give useful coverage at 30–40 psi, which is what a residential tap actually delivers with several heads open.

features.label: Dry storage
features.detail: Heads come off in seconds and live in a bin the rest of the year, so nothing sits on the house degrading in UV.

costs.upfront: CAD $700–$2,400 / USD $550–$1,900 depending on head count and hose length
costs.consumables: None. Water is the only running cost — roughly 1,200–2,500 L per hour for a full roofline, which matters if you are on a well or a cistern.
costs.ancillary: Budget CAD $150–$400 for extra hose and a Y-splitter or two if your taps are badly placed. If you want it to work when the hydrants drop, add a pump and tank — that is CAD $2,000–$8,000 and is the real cost of this category.
costs.fiveYear: Effectively the purchase price. Heads are plastic and replaceable individually at CAD $60–$120 each.

differentiators.label: Versus Platypus
differentiators.detail: WASP installs faster and is stocked more widely in Canada. Platypus throws further per head and is better on steep or complex rooflines, and costs a little more.

differentiators.label: Versus a tripod sprinkler
differentiators.detail: A $60 tripod wets the yard and a bit of wall. It does not put water on the roof deck, which is where embers land. Different job, tenth the price.

differentiators.label: Versus Frontline
differentiators.detail: Frontline is permanent, pump-fed and can be triggered from your phone from 400 km away. WASP requires you to be home with time to spare. That is the whole difference, and it is a big one.

differentiators.label: What it is not
differentiators.detail: This is not a fire-suppression system and no insurer will discount your premium for it. It is ember mitigation.

buying.lead: In stock most of the year; expect 2–6 week backorders from June through August
buying.where: Direct from WASP's Canadian store, through Flash Wildfire Services, and via a handful of rural hardware co-ops in BC and Alberta. US buyers generally order direct and pay cross-border shipping.
buying.note: Buy in the winter. Every Canadian supplier in this category sells out the week a major fire makes national news, and the backorder queue does not care that you are the one under the smoke column.

install.time: 45–90 minutes for a typical bungalow, first time
tools: Optional: hose clamps for tidy routing
install.note: The install itself is genuinely easy. The part people underestimate is the dry run: you need to actually turn it on once, walk the perimeter, and find the two corners the spray does not reach. Do that in April, not in August.

ongoing.note: Test it every spring and re-run the coverage walk. Heads go back in the bin after fire season. If you leave them clipped on year-round, expect UV embrittlement in 3–5 years.

alternatives.name: Platypus Roof Sprinkler
alternatives.note: Better throw, better on steep roofs, slightly fiddlier to mount.

alternatives.name: Tripod impact sprinklers
alternatives.note: A tenth the cost, a fraction of the protection. Worth owning as a supplement for the yard and fence line regardless.

alternatives.name: Frontline or a local installer's permanent system
alternatives.note: Ten to twenty times the price, and the only option if you may not be home when it matters.

guide.verdict: The default first sprinkler purchase for a Canadian homeowner who will be on site. Its real weakness is not the product, it is the water supply behind it — which is why we keep telling people to buy the pump before they buy the fancier heads.

name: Frontline Wildfire Defense System
pick: Best installed system
priceNote: Professionally installed; quote-based
summary: Permanently installed roof sprinkler system with its own pump, water storage and app-based remote activation. Coats the home in a foam-water mix that clings to surfaces. Aimed at high-value homes in California and the Western US.
pros: Remote activation from anywhere
Integrated water storage and pump
Firefighting foam adds surface protection
cons: Expensive
Requires professional install
US-only service area
bestFor: Owners who won't be home when a fire arrives and want automation.

guide.howItWorks: A permanently installed system: sprinkler heads mounted to the roof, ridge or eaves and plumbed with rigid pipe, fed by a dedicated pump drawing from a tank, pool or well, with a controller that you trigger from a phone app. You are buying the ability to turn the house on from wherever the evacuation order caught you.
guide.market: Permanent residential wildfire sprinkler systems are a genuine industry now, roughly $15,000–$40,000 installed, with Frontline the best-known North American brand and a growing set of regional installers building equivalent systems from off-the-shelf components. The market splits between brand-name packaged systems (Frontline, a few US competitors) and custom builds by local fire-protection contractors, who are often 20–30% cheaper for equivalent hardware but vary enormously in design competence. There is no certification standard for residential wildfire sprinkler design, which means the installer's judgment is the product you are actually buying.

features.label: Remote activation
features.detail: Cellular or satellite controller lets you start the system from anywhere. This is the entire reason the category exists.

features.label: Dedicated water source
features.detail: Sized to run 2–6 hours unassisted from a tank, cistern, pool or well — independent of municipal pressure, which is the thing that fails during a major fire.

features.label: Permanent plumbing
features.detail: No setup time, no ladder, nothing to forget. Freeze protection via drain-down or heat trace, depending on your climate.

features.label: Full-perimeter design
features.detail: A site survey drives head placement across roof, deck, outbuildings and the vulnerable wall sections — not just the front elevation.

features.label: Monitoring
features.detail: Most packages report pump status, tank level and pressure so you know it actually ran, rather than hoping.

costs.upfront: CAD $20,000–$55,000 / USD $15,000–$40,000 installed for a typical single-family home. Larger or multi-building properties run well past that.
costs.consumables: Pump fuel or power. A propane or diesel pump burns CAD $30–$80 per run.
costs.ancillary: If you do not already have a tank or a pool, the water storage is often 25–40% of the total. Some sites also need electrical work for the controller and pump.
costs.fiveYear: Budget CAD $500–$1,200 a year for annual commissioning, pump service and winterisation. Systems that are not serviced do not start.

differentiators.label: Versus every clip-on kit
differentiators.detail: The clip-on kits require a person, a ladder and an hour. This requires a phone. If you travel, work away, or have any realistic chance of being ordered out before you can get home, that is the whole argument.

differentiators.label: Versus a custom local build
differentiators.detail: Frontline gives you a known design, a warranty and a support line. A good local fire-protection contractor gives you the same hardware for less and knows your water table. A bad one gives you an expensive lawn sprinkler on the roof.

differentiators.label: Insurance
differentiators.detail: A small but growing number of Canadian insurers will discuss terms on a professionally installed and documented system in a high-risk postal code. Ask before you buy, get it in writing, and do not assume.

differentiators.label: Resale
differentiators.detail: In BC and Alberta interface communities this is starting to appear in listings as a feature. In most markets it is not yet a recoverable investment.

buying.lead: 6–16 weeks from first call to commissioning, longer if the water source needs work
buying.where: Frontline direct or through their authorised installer network; regional wildfire-protection contractors for custom builds.
buying.note: Get three quotes and make each one show you head placement on a site plan and the calculated run time from your actual water source. If a quote does not contain a run-time number, it is not an engineered system, it is a price.

install.time: 2–5 days on site, plus permitting and water-source work
tools: Nothing — this is a contractor install
install.note: Homeowner installation is not realistic and would void the warranty. Expect roof penetrations, a pump pad, electrical and possibly a plumbing permit.

ongoing.note: Annual service before fire season, winterisation after. Test-fire it yourself in the spring — do not take the app's word for it. This is the category where 'installed and forgotten' fails most often.

alternatives.name: Clip-on kit plus a portable pump and tank
alternatives.note: Roughly a fifth of the cost, most of the wetting, none of the remote activation. The right answer for most people.

alternatives.name: A local fire-protection contractor's custom system
alternatives.note: Often 20–30% less for the same hardware. Quality of design varies wildly — vet hard.

guide.verdict: Worth it if you are absent-risk: a second property, a job that takes you away in August, or a road out that closes early. If you will reliably be home with two hours' warning, the money is better spent on vents, a pump and Zone 0.

name: Platypus Roof Sprinkler
pick: Best roof-peak head
priceNote: Sold per head; typical home needs 2–4
summary: A brass roof-ridge sprinkler that straddles the peak and throws a wide circular pattern over both roof slopes. Originally from Australia, where roof sprinklers are standard in bushfire zones.
pros: All-metal construction survives radiant heat
Wide coverage per head
Semi-permanent mount stays in place all season
cons: Needs ladder access to install
Higher flow demand per head
bestFor: Single-storey homes with a simple gable roof.

guide.howItWorks: A single high-throw sprinkler head, usually ridge- or gutter-mounted, that puts a wide wetted circle over the roof from fewer positions than a clip-kit needs. You buy heads individually and place them to cover the roof with overlap, then feed them from a garden hose or a pump.
guide.market: Single-head roof sprinklers are the value tier of purpose-built wildfire wetting — the space between a $60 lawn tripod and a $1,500 multi-head kit. Buyers here are people who want real roof coverage but are willing to do the geometry themselves. Competition is mostly Canadian and mostly small: Platypus, several Alberta-built equivalents, and a long tail of no-name imports that look similar and throw half as far. The specification that separates them is wetted diameter at 40 psi, which the serious brands publish and the imports do not.

features.label: High throw per head
features.detail: A well-placed head covers 12–18 m diameter at residential pressure, so two or three can cover a small roof.

features.label: Buy individually
features.detail: No kit markup. Scale one head at a time as budget allows.

features.label: Ridge or gutter mount
features.detail: More placement freedom than a gutter-only clip, which matters on hipped and multi-level roofs.

features.label: Low-pressure design
features.detail: Rated to give useful coverage from a standard tap, and to work properly when you upgrade to a pump.

features.label: Metal internals on the better models
features.detail: Worth paying for. Plastic bearings in an impact head are the first thing to fail after two seasons of hard water.

costs.upfront: CAD $120–$350 per head. A typical bungalow needs 2–4; a two-storey with a complex roof, 4–6.
costs.consumables: None beyond water — roughly 400–900 L/hour per head.
costs.ancillary: Hose and splitters, CAD $100–$300. Mounting brackets if you ridge-mount rather than clip.
costs.fiveYear: Purchase price plus the occasional replacement head. Cheaper over five years than most kits.

differentiators.label: Versus WASP
differentiators.detail: Better throw, better on steep and irregular roofs, cheaper per unit of coverage. Costs you the design work — you have to figure out placement yourself instead of following a kit diagram.

differentiators.label: Versus a hardware-store impact sprinkler
differentiators.detail: Same operating principle, roughly triple the throw at low pressure and built to survive being run wide open for six hours. The cheap one will stall at 30 psi with three heads open.

differentiators.label: The pressure trap
differentiators.detail: Two heads on one tap is fine. Five is not — pressure divides and every head throws short. This is the single most common mistake in this category, and it is why the pump matters more than the head.

buying.lead: Usually in stock; summer shortages are common
buying.where: Direct from the manufacturer, Canadian wildfire equipment suppliers such as Flash Wildfire Services, and some rural farm-supply stores.
buying.note: Ask for the wetted-diameter figure at 40 psi before you buy. If nobody will give you one, buy something else.

install.time: 15–30 minutes per head once you have decided placement
install.note: Decide placement with the sprinkler running, on a calm day in spring, and mark the spots. Chalk the dry patches on the roof and move a head until they close up.

ongoing.note: Flush after each season — mineral scale is what kills impact heads. Store dry. Retest each spring.

alternatives.name: WASP full kit
alternatives.note: Faster to install, easier to get right, more money.

alternatives.name: Tripod impact sprinklers
alternatives.note: For the yard, fence line and outbuildings. Not for the roof.

guide.verdict: The best value per litre on the roof, if you are willing to spend an afternoon in the spring working out where the heads go. Pair with a pump before you buy a fourth head.

name: Brass Impact Sprinkler on Tripod
pick: Budget pick
priceNote: Commodity item; buy two or three
summary: A hardware-store brass impact sprinkler on an adjustable tripod, aimed at walls and decks, is the cheapest exterior wetting you can set up. Not a roof solution, but a real improvement for the Zone 0 perimeter.
pros: Very cheap and available everywhere
Covers deck, siding and the 1.5 m zone
Reusable for lawn watering
cons: Does not wet the roof
Plastic tripods deform in heat — choose metal
bestFor: Renters and anyone wanting an immediate, low-cost improvement.

guide.howItWorks: A brass impact sprinkler on an adjustable tripod — the same thing farms have used for eighty years. You place it upwind of what you want wet: the fence line, the deck, the woodpile, the outbuilding, the last few metres of yard. It will also put water on a low single-storey roof if you get the height and angle right.
guide.market: This is a commodity. Brass impact heads and tripods are made by dozens of manufacturers and sold through every hardware and farm-supply chain in North America, at CAD $40–$140. The only meaningful split is brass versus plastic internals: brass heads cost twice as much and last roughly ten times as long under continuous use. Nothing in this category is designed for wildfire specifically, and no vendor should be charging you a wildfire premium for one.

features.label: Adjustable arc and radius
features.detail: Set full circle or a part-arc so you are not wasting pressure watering the road.

features.label: Tripod height
features.detail: Most extend to 1.2–1.8 m, which is enough to clear a fence and reach a low roof edge.

features.label: Brass internals
features.detail: The whole quality question. Brass survives being run wide open for hours; plastic bearings do not.

features.label: Standard hose thread
features.detail: Works with everything you already own, and chains in series if pressure allows.

costs.upfront: CAD $40–$140 each. Two or three is a sensible number.
costs.consumables: None. About 500–1,000 L/hour each.
costs.ancillary: Hose, splitters and quick-connects: CAD $60–$200.
costs.fiveYear: A brass unit run a few hours a year will outlive the fence it is protecting.

differentiators.label: Versus roof sprinklers
differentiators.detail: Completely different job. This wets ground fuel, fences and structures at ground level. It does not reliably wet a roof deck, which is where the ember problem lives. Own both; do not substitute.

differentiators.label: Brass versus plastic
differentiators.detail: Pay the extra CAD $50. A plastic head that seizes in hour three of the only day it mattered was not a saving.

differentiators.label: The honest caveat
differentiators.detail: Wetting the yard has real but modest value — it slows surface spread and buys minutes. It will not stop a crown fire and it will not save a house with open vents.

buying.lead: Same day, almost anywhere
buying.where: Any hardware store, farm supply, irrigation supplier or Amazon.
buying.note: The easiest purchase on this entire site. Buy it this weekend and stop thinking about it.

install.time: 5 minutes
install.note: None required. Set it up, spread the legs, connect, done.

ongoing.note: Drain and store indoors over winter. Occasional nozzle clean if you are on well water.

alternatives.name: Platypus or WASP roof sprinklers
alternatives.note: For the roof. This is not a substitute.

alternatives.name: Soaker hose along a fence line
alternatives.note: Cheaper still, far less water thrown, useful for a specific hot spot.

guide.verdict: Cheap, useful, and not to be confused with roof protection. Buy two, use them on the fence line, the woodpile and the shed, and spend your real money higher up the priority list.

name: Phos-Chek Wildfire Home Defense
pick: Best long-term retardant
priceNote: 1-gal concentrate with hose-end sprayer
summary: The consumer version of the red retardant dropped from air tankers. Applied days or weeks ahead to fences, decks, mulch and siding; stays effective until rinsed by heavy rain. Dries clear.
pros: Apply early — no last-minute scramble
Same chemistry as aerial retardant
Dries clear on most surfaces
cons: Washes off in rain
Covers surfaces, not the whole structure
bestFor: Seasonal treatment of fences, wood decks and mulch beds.

guide.howItWorks: A long-term retardant concentrate you mix with water and spray on fences, decks, mulch beds, sheds and the wooden things around the house. Unlike gel, it does not depend on staying wet: the salts stay on the surface after the water evaporates and chemically interfere with combustion for weeks or months, until heavy rain washes them off. You apply it early in the season, not at the last minute.
guide.market: Consumer long-term retardant is a young category dominated by one name — Phos-Chek, the same Perimeter Solutions chemistry dropped from air tankers, repackaged for homeowners. Competitors are mostly regional resellers of similar ammonium-phosphate formulations, plus a fringe of unregistered products that are essentially fertiliser with dye. The meaningful buying signal is regulatory: in the US, look for a product on the USDA Forest Service qualified products list; in Canada, check the PMRA registration or the manufacturer's Canadian SDS. Anything sold as 'fire retardant' with no registration number is a bottle of salt water.

features.label: Long-term protection
features.detail: Stays effective after drying — typically until roughly 25–50 mm of cumulative rain has fallen. One spring application often covers most of a dry season.

features.label: Concentrate
features.detail: Sold as powder or liquid concentrate, mixed at the labelled ratio in a pump sprayer or hose-end applicator.

features.label: Coloured or uncoloured
features.detail: The uncoloured version is far more sensible on a house. The coloured version exists so aerial crews can see coverage, and it will stain.

features.label: Broad substrate compatibility
features.detail: Wood, mulch, vegetation, fencing. Not for glass, vehicles or anything you want to keep clean.

costs.upfront: CAD $120–$350 / USD $90–$280 for a homeowner kit covering roughly 200–500 m² of surface, depending on absorbency.
costs.consumables: The retardant itself is the consumable. Budget one full application per season, twice if you get a wet June.
costs.ancillary: A 15–20 L backpack or wheeled pump sprayer, CAD $80–$250, if you do not already own one. Gloves and eye protection.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $600–$1,800 for a house that reapplies annually. This is a subscription, not a purchase — plan for it.

differentiators.label: Versus gel
differentiators.detail: The fundamental split in this category. Retardant is applied weeks ahead and keeps working dry. Gel is applied in the last hour and only works while it is wet. They are complementary, not competing — retardant on the fence in May, gel on the wall in August.

differentiators.label: Versus doing nothing to the fence
differentiators.detail: A wooden fence that runs up to the house is one of the most reliable ways to deliver fire to a wall. Treating it is high-value. Replacing the last 2 m with metal is better and permanent.

differentiators.label: The staining question
differentiators.detail: Even uncoloured product can leave a faint residue on cedar and light stone. Test a patch. Assume you will be pressure-washing something afterwards.

differentiators.label: Environmental note
differentiators.detail: Ammonium-phosphate retardants are hard on fish. Do not spray near a creek, pond or storm drain, and keep it out of the ditch.

buying.lead: Usually in stock spring and early summer; sells out during active fire seasons
buying.where: Direct from Perimeter Solutions' consumer channel, Amazon in both countries, and Canadian wildfire equipment suppliers. Some rural fire departments run bulk-buy programs — worth a phone call.
buying.note: Check the label for a registration number before you pay. This category attracts imitators.

install.time: 2–4 hours for a typical property, plus mixing
install.note: Do it on a calm, dry day with 24 hours of no rain forecast. Mask anything you care about — windows, siding, vehicles, the neighbour's car. Work top-down and do not skimp on the fence sections nearest the house, which are the ones that matter.

ongoing.note: Reapply after heavy rain and at least once a year. Diarise it for the first dry week of spring. Store the concentrate dry and above freezing.

alternatives.name: Barricade or Thermo-Gel
alternatives.note: Different job — last-hour wet protection, not season-long dry protection.

alternatives.name: Replacing the last 2 m of wooden fence with steel
alternatives.note: CAD $200–$600 and permanent. Do this as well, and it removes the reason to spray that section at all.

guide.verdict: The highest-value chemical purchase for most properties, because it treats the fences, decks and mulch that actually carry fire to the wall. Just understand you are signing up for an annual chore, not buying a thing once.

name: Barricade Fire Blocking Gel
pick: Best last-minute gel
priceNote: Sold in 1-gal jugs and 5-gal home kits with applicator
summary: A superabsorbent polymer gel that clings to vertical surfaces and holds a water barrier for hours. Used by fire departments; the home kit includes a hose-end applicator. Apply when evacuation is ordered.
pros: Proven in departmental use
Clings to siding, windows and decks
Hose-end applicator included in kits
cons: Effective window is 6–24 hours
Cleanup after the fact takes work
Needs ~40 psi water pressure
bestFor: Homes in the path of an approaching fire with an hour to spare.

guide.howItWorks: A superabsorbent polymer concentrate that mixes with water into a thick gel and is sprayed onto walls, windows, decks and eaves. The gel is roughly 99% water held in a matrix that resists running off and evaporating. It buys the surface it covers a window of protection — typically a few hours in serious heat — and stops working the moment it dries out. It is the last thing you do before you leave.
guide.market: Fire-blocking gel is a small, technically genuine category with three or four credible manufacturers — Barricade, Thermo-Gel, and a couple of firefighting-supply brands — plus a great deal of marketing noise. All the real products are variations on the same polymer chemistry, tested to broadly similar standards, and used by professional structure-protection crews. Consumer pricing is CAD $150–$600 for enough concentrate to treat one house once. The differentiators between brands are dwell time in heat, ease of mixing, and whether you can apply it with a garden hose eductor or need a dedicated pump.

features.label: Hose-end application
features.detail: Barricade's consumer kit uses an eductor that meters concentrate into a garden hose stream — no separate mixing tank, no pump required.

features.label: Cling on vertical surfaces
features.detail: The whole point. It stays on a wall or a window where water would run off in seconds.

features.label: Rewettable
features.detail: If it starts to dry and you still have water and time, you can wet it again rather than reapplying concentrate.

features.label: Non-toxic, water-soluble
features.detail: Rinses off with a pressure washer afterwards. Safe on painted siding, though it will need cleaning up.

costs.upfront: CAD $250–$700 / USD $200–$550 for a homeowner kit — concentrate plus eductor — covering roughly one full application on an average house.
costs.consumables: The concentrate. One serious application empties a homeowner kit. Assume you buy a replacement after every use.
costs.ancillary: Adequate water pressure and volume. If your tap cannot sustain flow, add a pump. A second person makes the application twice as fast, which matters when you have an hour.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $250–$700 for the kit plus a replacement after any use. Shelf life is typically 3–5 years — check the date and replace expired stock.

differentiators.label: Versus Phos-Chek retardant
differentiators.detail: Gel works wet and is applied at the last minute; retardant works dry and is applied in spring. You want both, for different surfaces at different times.

differentiators.label: Versus Thermo-Gel
differentiators.detail: Broadly equivalent chemistry. Barricade's consumer packaging and hose eductor are easier for a homeowner; Thermo-Gel's larger formats are cheaper per litre and aimed at people with a pump.

differentiators.label: The timing trap
differentiators.detail: Gel applied too early has dried out and is doing nothing by the time the front arrives. Gel applied too late means you were still on a ladder when you should have been driving. This product demands that you have a plan and a trigger point written down.

differentiators.label: What it cannot do
differentiators.detail: It protects the surfaces you covered. It does nothing for an open vent, a gutter full of needles, or a woodpile against the wall.

buying.lead: In stock most of the year, scarce during active fire seasons
buying.where: Barricade direct, Amazon in both countries, Canadian wildfire equipment suppliers, and firefighting supply houses.
buying.note: Buy the concentrate and the eductor together. Check the expiry date on arrival — this category moves slowly through retail and old stock is common.

install.time: 45–90 minutes to apply to a full house under pressure, if you have practised
install.note: Practise once with plain water so you know the reach, the sequence and how long it actually takes. Applying gel for the first time on the day of an evacuation order is how people get caught out. Prioritise: windows and glazed doors first, then walls facing the fuel, then the deck.

ongoing.note: Check the expiry date each spring. Rinse thoroughly after any application. Replace the kit after use — do not assume half a jug is a second defence.

alternatives.name: Thermo-Gel 200L
alternatives.note: Cheaper per litre in bulk, better if you have a pump and a large property.

alternatives.name: Exterior sprinklers
alternatives.note: Run unattended for hours rather than needing a person with a wand. Different failure mode — they need water pressure to keep flowing.

guide.verdict: A real product that does a real thing, and one that punishes poor planning more than anything else on this site. Only buy it if you will also write down the trigger point at which you start spraying — and the later trigger point at which you stop and drive.

name: Thermo-Gel 200L
pick: Runner-up gel
priceNote: Concentrate; needs an eductor or hose-end applicator
summary: Another fire-department-grade gel concentrate. Slightly cheaper per litre than Barricade but the applicator is sold separately. Good choice if you already own a foam eductor.
pros: Cost-effective in volume
Long shelf life as concentrate
cons: Applicator sold separately
Harder to find in Canada
bestFor: Property owners protecting multiple buildings.

guide.howItWorks: The same superabsorbent-polymer principle as Barricade, sold in the volume a structure-protection crew or a large rural property actually uses. You draw concentrate through an eductor or inject it into a pump discharge, and coat structures with gel that holds water against heat for hours.
guide.market: This is the professional end of the gel market, where the buyer is a rural fire department, a contractor doing structure protection, or a homeowner with several buildings and a pump. Per-litre cost drops sharply above about 20 L, and 200 L drums are the standard format. Thermo-Gel and Barricade both compete here alongside firefighting distributors' house brands. Performance differences between credible brands are smaller than the differences in how well the operator applies the product.

features.label: Bulk economics
features.detail: Per-litre cost is typically a third to a half of consumer kit pricing.

features.label: Pump-fed application
features.detail: Designed to be injected into a pump discharge or drawn by a proportioner, which is how you cover multiple buildings in the time available.

features.label: Long dwell in heat
features.detail: Formulated to hold water under radiant load rather than flash off, which is the specification that matters and the one worth asking about.

features.label: Multi-structure coverage
features.detail: A drum treats a house, barn, shop and a pump house, with margin.

costs.upfront: CAD $2,500–$6,000 / USD $2,000–$4,500 for a 200 L drum, varying widely by distributor and season.
costs.consumables: The drum is the consumable. Shelf life is typically 3–5 years unopened, less once broached.
costs.ancillary: A pump and proportioner or eductor, CAD $1,500–$6,000, and hose. Without those this is a drum of expensive syrup.
costs.fiveYear: Assume a drum replacement per five-year cycle even if unused, plus pump service.

differentiators.label: Versus a consumer gel kit
differentiators.detail: Far cheaper per litre and the only sensible option above about three structures. Requires equipment and a person who has trained with it.

differentiators.label: Versus retardant
differentiators.detail: Same wet-versus-dry distinction as always. Bulk gel does not remove the case for treating fences in spring.

differentiators.label: Who this is actually for
differentiators.detail: Ranches, acreages with outbuildings, remote lodges, and neighbourhood co-operatives who buy one drum and one pump between six houses. If you have one house on a suburban lot, buy the consumer kit.

buying.lead: 1–6 weeks; dangerous-goods shipping applies and drums are not couriered casually
buying.where: Firefighting supply distributors, wildfire equipment specialists, and direct from the manufacturer for volume orders.
buying.note: Ask about freight before you commit — drum shipping to a rural address can add CAD $300–$800. A shared purchase with neighbours is the standard way people afford this.

install.time: Application of a full property: 2–4 hours with a trained operator
install.note: This is equipment, not a product you unbox. Budget a training day with whoever sold it to you, and run a water-only drill annually. The failure mode here is a drum nobody knows how to deploy.

ongoing.note: Annual drill, pump service, drum date check. Store above freezing and out of sunlight.

alternatives.name: Barricade consumer kit
alternatives.note: The right size for a single house. Ten times simpler.

alternatives.name: Hiring a structure-protection contractor on standby
alternatives.note: Some BC and Alberta operators sell pre-season agreements. Worth pricing against buying the drum yourself.

guide.verdict: Correct for acreages, ranches and neighbourhood co-ops — wrong for a single suburban house, where the consumer kit does the same job without demanding you become a pump operator.

name: Vulcan Ember-Resistant Vents
pick: Best attic & soffit vent
priceNote: Per vent; typical home needs 8–20
summary: WUI-listed vents with an intumescent honeycomb that expands and seals at roughly 350°F, plus 1/8 in mesh. Available in soffit, gable, foundation and dormer formats in standard sizes.
pros: Intumescent seal blocks flame, not just embers
Full range of sizes
California WUI listed
cons: Pricier than mesh-only vents
Once activated, vents must be replaced
bestFor: Whole-house vent replacement.

guide.howItWorks: A replacement vent that looks like a normal soffit, gable or foundation vent until it gets hot. Inside is an intumescent material that expands when exposed to fire or high heat and plugs the opening completely, sealing the attic or crawlspace against embers and flame. The rest of the year it ventilates normally, which is the whole trick — you cannot simply block a vent, because the building needs the airflow.
guide.market: Ember-resistant vents are a small but maturing market driven almost entirely by California building code. Chapter 7A of the California Building Code and the associated WUI listings created the demand, and the credible manufacturers — Vulcan, Brandguard, and a handful of others — all build to that standard. Prices run CAD $60–$220 per vent. Outside California there is no code requirement anywhere in North America yet, which means the market is entirely voluntary and most homeowners have never heard of the product. That is unfortunate, because attic vents are the single most common route by which embers get inside a house.

features.label: Intumescent closure
features.detail: Expands and seals under heat. Passive, no power, no maintenance, nothing to activate.

features.label: Normal ventilation when cold
features.detail: Net free area comparable to the vent it replaces, so you do not create a moisture problem in the attic.

features.label: WUI listing
features.detail: Tested to California's Chapter 7A ember-intrusion and flame-impingement protocols. This is the only meaningful third-party validation in the category — ask for the listing number.

features.label: Standard sizes
features.detail: Made in common North American vent dimensions so most swaps are drop-in.

features.label: Multiple types
features.detail: Soffit, gable, dormer, foundation and roof vents — you generally need a mix.

costs.upfront: CAD $70–$220 per vent. A typical bungalow has 8–20 vents; a two-storey with a complex roof, 20–40.
costs.consumables: None. Passive device, no service parts.
costs.ancillary: Cross-border shipping if buying US product into Canada, plus duty. Paint if you want them to match.
costs.fiveYear: Nil. This is genuinely buy-once.

differentiators.label: Versus 1/8 in ember mesh
differentiators.detail: Mesh is a tenth the price and stops the majority of embers. It does not stop flame impingement and it does not seal. If budget is tight, mesh everything first — then upgrade the two or three vents most exposed to the fuel.

differentiators.label: Versus Brandguard
differentiators.detail: Broadly equivalent performance and price. Brandguard uses a baffle-and-mesh geometry, Vulcan an intumescent plug. Vulcan tends to be easier to source in Canada; availability should probably decide it for you.

differentiators.label: Versus blocking vents with plywood on the day
differentiators.detail: People plan this and then are not home, or are home and forget the crawlspace. A passive device does not depend on you.

differentiators.label: The under-appreciated point
differentiators.detail: Vents are where houses actually get lost. Post-fire investigations keep finding intact exteriors with burned-out attics. This is not a glamorous purchase and it may be the highest-leverage one on the site.

buying.lead: 2–6 weeks typical; longer for non-standard sizes
buying.where: Vulcan direct, WUI-focused building suppliers, and a growing number of Canadian building-supply dealers. Many are ordered rather than stocked.
buying.note: Count and measure every vent on the house before you call — soffit, gable, roof, foundation, dryer and crawlspace. People routinely order for the ones they can see and discover four more later.

install.time: 15–40 minutes per vent; a full house is a weekend or a day for a contractor
install.note: Soffit vents are straightforward if you are comfortable on a ladder. Gable and roof vents are less so. Most homeowners do the soffits themselves and hire out the roof. Budget CAD $600–$2,000 for a contractor to do a whole house.

ongoing.note: Inspect annually for paint over-spray blocking the vent and for wasp nests. Otherwise nothing.

alternatives.name: Brandguard Ember & Flame Vents
alternatives.note: Equivalent alternative; buy whichever you can actually get.

alternatives.name: 1/8 in stainless ember mesh
alternatives.note: A tenth the cost, most of the benefit for embers, none of it for flame. A legitimate stepping stone.

guide.verdict: The best money on this site per dollar of risk removed, and the one nobody buys because it is invisible. If you do one structural upgrade, do the vents.

name: Brandguard Ember & Flame Vents
pick: Best baffle-style vent
priceNote: Per vent
summary: Uses a patented baffle design to stop embers without relying on fine mesh that clogs. Good airflow numbers and a wide catalogue of eave, gable and foundation models.
pros: High net free area (airflow)
Baffle design resists clogging
WUI listed
cons: Some models are deeper than the vents they replace
bestFor: Homes where attic ventilation is already marginal.

guide.howItWorks: A vent built as a labyrinth: incoming air has to turn through a baffled path lined with fine mesh before it reaches the attic. Embers, which travel in a straight line and burn out quickly, cannot make the turns. Flame is stopped by the mesh and the geometry. There is no expanding material and no activation — the shape of the thing is the mechanism.
guide.market: Brandguard is one of the two names that come up whenever ember-resistant vents are discussed, alongside Vulcan, and both were built for California's Chapter 7A market. Pricing sits in the same CAD $80–$250 per vent band. The category as a whole is under-bought outside California and dramatically under-marketed — there is no advertising budget behind attic vents, which is why most homeowners in high-risk Canadian postal codes have never encountered the concept.

features.label: Baffled labyrinth path
features.detail: Passive geometry — nothing to expand, degrade or expire.

features.label: Integral fine mesh
features.detail: Corrosion-resistant mesh inside the baffle path, protected from physical damage by the housing.

features.label: WUI listed
features.detail: Tested to California Chapter 7A protocols. Ask for the listing number; it is the category's only real third-party check.

features.label: Full product range
features.detail: Soffit, eave, gable, foundation, dormer and roof configurations in common sizes.

features.label: Paintable
features.detail: Finished to accept paint so it disappears into the soffit line.

costs.upfront: CAD $80–$250 per vent. Budget by count: 8–20 vents on a bungalow, 20–40 on a larger two-storey.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: Freight and duty on US-sourced product. Paint.
costs.fiveYear: Nil beyond an annual look.

differentiators.label: Versus Vulcan
differentiators.detail: Different mechanism, similar tested outcome, similar price. The baffle design has no material that could theoretically age out; the intumescent design gives a positive seal rather than a filtered path. Neither difference is large enough to override availability and lead time in your area.

differentiators.label: Versus mesh alone
differentiators.detail: Mesh retrofits are cheap and worthwhile. A listed vent also handles direct flame impingement, which mesh over a plain vent does not.

differentiators.label: Net free area
differentiators.detail: Any restrictive vent reduces airflow. Check that your replacement's net free area meets your attic's ventilation requirement, or you are trading a fire problem for a moisture and ice-dam problem.

buying.lead: 2–8 weeks; often a special order in Canada
buying.where: Brandguard direct, WUI building suppliers, specialist distributors. Some Canadian FireSmart-affiliated contractors will source them as part of a package.
buying.note: Get a full vent schedule — type, size and count — before ordering. Mixed sizes are normal and a second freight charge for four missed vents is annoying.

install.time: 15–40 minutes per vent
install.note: Same as any vent swap: remove the old, check the rough opening, fit, seal the perimeter. Roof-mounted units are a roofer's job unless you are genuinely comfortable up there.

ongoing.note: Annual visual check for blockage, paint over-spray and nests.

alternatives.name: Vulcan Vents
alternatives.note: The direct equivalent. Choose on lead time.

alternatives.name: Stainless ember mesh over existing vents
alternatives.note: The budget path, and a reasonable one.

guide.verdict: Interchangeable with Vulcan for practical purposes. Order whichever one you can get in the size mix your house actually needs, and do not let a preference between two good products become a reason to do nothing for another season.

name: 1/8 in Stainless Steel Ember Mesh
pick: Budget retrofit
priceNote: Sold by the roll
summary: A roll of 1/8 in (3 mm) stainless mesh stapled or screwed over existing vents is the recommended retrofit when replacement isn't practical. Also use it to close gaps under decks and at the base of siding.
pros: Cheapest effective ember defense
Covers decks, gaps and odd-size vents
Stainless won't rust or burn
cons: Does not seal against flame contact
Reduces airflow somewhat
bestFor: Renters, older homes, and under-deck screening.

guide.howItWorks: 1/8 inch (3 mm) stainless steel woven mesh, cut and fastened over the inside or outside of existing vents, under-deck openings, crawlspace access and any other gap an ember could enter. The aperture is the entire specification: 3 mm is small enough to stop the vast majority of wind-carried embers and large enough not to choke ventilation or clog with dust.
guide.market: A commodity material sold by screen suppliers, hardware chains, industrial mesh distributors and Amazon, at CAD $40–$150 per roll. The only questions are aperture and alloy. Aluminium mesh is cheaper and melts. Fibreglass insect screen is useless — it burns. 1/4 inch hardware cloth passes embers. Get 1/8 inch stainless, usually type 304 or 316, and ignore everything else on the shelf.

features.label: 1/8 in aperture
features.detail: The figure recommended by FireSmart Canada, NFPA and California Chapter 7A. Not 1/4 in, which passes embers, and not window screen, which clogs.

features.label: Stainless steel
features.detail: Will not melt under flame contact and will not corrode out in five years the way galvanised does in coastal or road-salt conditions.

features.label: Cuts with snips
features.detail: No special tooling. Fastens with staples, screws and washers, or a wooden batten.

features.label: Universal application
features.detail: Vents, under-deck skirting, crawlspace openings, the gap under a shed, the space behind lattice.

costs.upfront: CAD $40–$150 per roll. One or two rolls covers a typical house.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: Stainless staples or screws and fender washers, CAD $20–$40. Use stainless fasteners — galvanised staples into stainless mesh corrode fast.
costs.fiveYear: Nil.

differentiators.label: Versus listed ember-resistant vents
differentiators.detail: A tenth the price and it addresses the dominant threat, which is wind-blown embers. It does not address direct flame impingement on the vent, and it does not seal. The sensible sequence for a tight budget is: mesh everything now, upgrade the most exposed vents to listed units later.

differentiators.label: Versus aluminium or fibreglass screen
differentiators.detail: Aluminium melts around 660 °C, which a burning vent easily exceeds. Fibreglass insect screen burns. Neither is a fire product regardless of what the packaging implies.

differentiators.label: The clogging myth
differentiators.detail: 1/8 in stainless does not meaningfully restrict attic ventilation on a normal house. It will collect lint at a dryer vent, so check that one annually.

differentiators.label: Do not forget
differentiators.detail: The openings people miss: under the deck, behind lattice skirting, the crawlspace hatch, the gap where the gas line enters, and the roof-to-wall junction on a split-level.

buying.lead: Same day to a week
buying.where: Hardware stores, industrial screen and mesh suppliers, Amazon in both countries, farm supply.
buying.note: Confirm the aperture in the listing, not the marketing name. 'Fine mesh' means nothing; 1/8 in or 3 mm means something.

install.time: A full afternoon to do a whole house properly
tools: Gloves — cut mesh edges are vicious
Staple gun with stainless staples or drill and screws
install.note: Fasten it on the inside of the vent where you can, so the exterior look is unchanged and the mesh is protected. Overlap generously and fasten every 100–150 mm — an edge that lifts is a hole. Wear gloves; this material draws blood.

ongoing.note: Annual walk-around looking for lifted edges, corrosion at fasteners and lint at the dryer vent.

alternatives.name: Vulcan or Brandguard vents
alternatives.note: The proper upgrade when budget allows. Do the mesh anyway on everything that is not a vent.

alternatives.name: Nothing
alternatives.note: The most common choice and the reason attics burn.

guide.verdict: The cheapest genuinely effective thing you can buy for a house. If you read one product page on this site and act on it, make it this one — CAD $60 and an afternoon closes the openings that lose houses.

name: Stainless Micro-Mesh Gutter Guard
pick: Best gutter guard
priceNote: Priced per linear foot; measure your gutters
summary: Stainless micro-mesh on an aluminum frame blocks pine needles and seeds while letting water through. Non-combustible by design, which is the whole point in a wildfire zone.
pros: Blocks pine needles
All-metal — will not ignite
DIY install with screws
cons: Needs occasional brushing
May interfere with gutter-clip sprinklers
bestFor: Homes under conifers.

guide.howItWorks: A stainless micro-mesh panel that clips or screws over the eavestrough so water gets in and needles, leaves and embers do not. The fire logic is simple: a gutter full of dry conifer litter sitting against the fascia is a ready-made ember trap at the exact point where roof meets wall. Keep the trough empty and you remove one of the most reliable ignition points on a house.
guide.market: Gutter protection is a large, noisy consumer market where most of the money is in installed systems sold door-to-door at CAD $2,500–$8,000 a house, with aggressive marketing and long warranties. Underneath that, the same stainless micro-mesh panels sell as DIY product for CAD $4–$12 per linear foot. The fire-relevant distinction is not brand, it is material and aperture: stainless micro-mesh over an aluminium frame is the only construction that both excludes conifer needles and cannot melt. Plastic and foam inserts are common, cheap, and actively bad here — foam holds debris and burns, and plastic deforms.

features.label: Stainless micro-mesh
features.detail: Fine enough to exclude pine and fir needles, which defeat every coarser design.

features.label: Non-combustible construction
features.detail: Stainless mesh on aluminium or steel frame. Nothing in the assembly burns or melts.

features.label: Clip or screw fixing
features.detail: Most DIY panels either snap under the first shingle course or screw to the front lip. Under-shingle fitting can affect a roof warranty — check.

features.label: Sold by the foot
features.detail: Measure your gutter run and buy that length. No package pricing games.

costs.upfront: CAD $6–$16 per linear foot DIY. A typical bungalow has 120–200 ft of gutter, so CAD $800–$3,000.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: Stainless screws. A ladder stabiliser if you do not have one, CAD $60–$120.
costs.fiveYear: Nil in materials. It saves you two gutter cleans a year, which is CAD $200–$500 annually if you were paying someone.

differentiators.label: Versus foam or brush inserts
differentiators.detail: Cheaper and worse. Foam holds needles and organic debris in the trough and is itself combustible. Brush inserts collect litter in the bristles. Both make the fire problem slightly worse while looking like a solution.

differentiators.label: Versus an installed premium system
differentiators.detail: Same functional material at a quarter to a third of the price. You are paying the difference for warranty, labour and not being on a ladder.

differentiators.label: Versus just cleaning the gutters twice a year
differentiators.detail: Free and equally effective — if you actually do it, every year, including the back of the house and the second storey. Most people do not. Guards are a hedge against your own future laziness, which is a legitimate thing to buy.

differentiators.label: Fire-season caveat
differentiators.detail: Guards keep the trough clear but debris still accumulates on top of them, on the roof and in valleys. They are not a reason to stop looking at your roof.

buying.lead: In stock; DIY panels ship in days
buying.where: Building-supply chains, roofing suppliers, Amazon, and gutter specialists. Installed systems via the usual home-improvement contractors.
buying.note: Ignore anything sold as a 'fire-rated gutter guard' at a premium — there is no such rating. What you want is stainless micro-mesh, which is a specification you can verify.

install.time: A full weekend for a typical house, DIY
install.note: The hard part is not the product, it is the hours on a ladder and the corners and downpipe transitions. If your house is two storeys or the roof pitch is steep, hire it out — falls are the actual risk in this project.

ongoing.note: Blow or brush debris off the top of the guards each autumn and again before fire season. Check the roof valleys at the same time, which is where the litter that matters usually sits.

alternatives.name: Twice-yearly gutter cleaning
alternatives.note: Free, equally effective, requires discipline you may not have.

alternatives.name: Metal gutter with no guard, cleaned before fire season
alternatives.note: Perfectly acceptable if the trees near the house are deciduous rather than conifer.

guide.verdict: Worth doing, mainly because it removes a maintenance task you were probably going to skip. Do not overpay for a branded installed system when the material that matters costs a third as much.

name: Firezat Fire Shield Structure Wrap
pick: Best structure wrap
priceNote: Sold by the roll; a cabin needs several
summary: Aluminized fibreglass wrap of the type used by the US Forest Service to protect historic cabins and lookouts. Reflects up to 95% of radiant heat. Realistic for sheds, cabins, pump houses and tank enclosures.
pros: Proven on real fires
Reflects radiant heat and blocks embers
Reusable if handled carefully
cons: Hours of labour and multiple people to install
Impractical for large homes
Must be sealed at every seam
bestFor: Cabins, outbuildings and anything you can wrap in an afternoon.

guide.howItWorks: A reflective aluminium-faced fabric that you fasten over the exterior of a structure before a fire front arrives. It reflects radiant heat and blocks direct ember contact with the wall and roof surfaces underneath. It is the same principle firefighters use when they wrap historic cabins and lookouts ahead of a burn — which is exactly where the technique comes from.
guide.market: Structure wrap is a genuinely proven technique with a very small consumer market. Firezat is the best-known homeowner-facing brand; the rest of the category is professional wrap sold to agencies for fire-line use. Consumer kits run CAD $3,500–$12,000 for a house. The problem is not efficacy — agencies use it because it works — it is deployment: wrapping a house is a multi-person job that takes hours, needs practice, and has to happen before the front arrives but after you would rather have left.

features.label: Reflective aluminium face
features.detail: Rejects the radiant heat that ignites siding, trim and window frames without any flame contact.

features.label: Fibreglass-reinforced substrate
features.detail: Strong enough to survive the wind and handling that wrapping a house involves.

features.label: Custom-cut kits
features.detail: Sold cut to your building's dimensions with a fastening scheme, rather than as a roll you improvise from.

features.label: Reusable
features.detail: If it is not damaged, it comes off and goes back in the crate for next time.

features.label: Covers what nothing else can
features.detail: Windows, eaves, decks and log walls all at once — surfaces that sprinklers and gel each only partly address.

costs.upfront: CAD $4,000–$14,000 / USD $3,000–$11,000 for a house kit, depending on size and complexity.
costs.consumables: Fasteners and tape per deployment, CAD $100–$300. Damaged panels after a real deployment.
costs.ancillary: Storage space. A crate of wrap is bulky and must stay dry.
costs.fiveYear: Purchase price plus replacement of damaged sections. Realistically, most kits are deployed zero or one times in five years.

differentiators.label: Versus gel
differentiators.detail: Wrap does not need water and does not dry out, so it holds indefinitely once up. It takes far longer to deploy and costs several times as much.

differentiators.label: Versus sprinklers
differentiators.detail: Sprinklers run unattended for hours but need water and pressure. Wrap needs neither but needs people and time. Neither substitutes for the other.

differentiators.label: The deployment problem
differentiators.detail: This is the honest issue with the category. Wrapping a two-storey house is a 4–8 hour job for two or three people with ladders, in smoke, under an evacuation order. If you have not rehearsed it, you will not complete it.

differentiators.label: Where it genuinely wins
differentiators.detail: Log homes, heritage cabins, remote structures with no water supply, and outbuildings you plan to wrap early and leave. Also the only good answer for a structure you can prepare days ahead and then walk away from.

buying.lead: 3–10 weeks — kits are made to your building's measurements
buying.where: Firezat direct and a small number of wildfire equipment specialists.
buying.note: You will need accurate elevation dimensions before ordering. Take photos of every face of the building and get the supplier to check your take-off.

install.time: 4–8 hours for a house with two to three people, if rehearsed. Longer the first time — much longer.
tools: A second and ideally third person
install.note: Rehearse it. Once, fully, on a calm spring day, with a stopwatch. If the rehearsal takes eleven hours you have learned something vital while it was still safe to learn it. Wrap the roof and the upwind elevation first if you run short of time.

ongoing.note: Keep it dry, keep the take-off diagram with the crate, and re-rehearse whenever the household changes — a two-person job becomes impossible when one person moves out.

alternatives.name: Barricade gel plus sprinklers
alternatives.note: Faster to deploy, needs water, comparable or better for a conventional house with a decent supply.

alternatives.name: Wrapping only the outbuilding or the exposed elevation
alternatives.note: A much smaller kit, a realistic deployment time, and most of the value if one face carries the risk.

guide.verdict: The technique works — agencies would not use it otherwise. Whether it works for you comes down to one question: can you and the people who will actually be present put it up in the time you will actually have? Answer that with a rehearsal, not with optimism.

name: Fire-Resistant Propane Tank Cover
pick: Cheap essential
priceNote: Sized for 20 lb and 100 lb cylinders
summary: A silica or aluminized cover for BBQ and heating propane cylinders. Tanks venting near a house are a major secondary ignition source; a cover buys time and reduces radiant heat on the tank.
pros: Inexpensive
Fits in a go-kit
Also protects tank from UV year-round
cons: Better solution is moving the tank 10 m from the house
bestFor: Everyone with a BBQ tank on the deck.

guide.howItWorks: A fire-resistant fabric cover, usually silicone- or aluminium-faced fibreglass, thrown over a propane tank or cylinder to shield it from radiant heat and ember contact. It buys the tank time before the pressure relief valve starts venting, and it keeps burning debris off the valve assembly and regulator.
guide.market: A small niche with a handful of manufacturers, mostly the same firms making welding blankets and industrial heat shields, plus a few wildfire-specific brands. Prices run CAD $80–$400 depending on tank size and material. Quality varies more than the price suggests: the fire-relevant spec is the fabric's continuous temperature rating and whether it is genuinely rated for radiant heat shielding or is a repurposed welding blanket sold at a wildfire markup.

features.label: Radiant heat shielding
features.detail: Reflective or high-emissivity face that keeps the tank body cooler for longer under radiant load.

features.label: Sized to common tanks
features.detail: 20 lb and 40 lb cylinders, 100 lb cylinders, and 250–500 gal horizontal tanks each need a different cover.

features.label: Vent-clear design
features.detail: The good ones leave the pressure relief valve unobstructed. A cover that blocks the PRV is worse than no cover.

features.label: Tie-down system
features.detail: Straps or grommets so it does not blow off in the wind that comes with a fire front.

costs.upfront: CAD $80–$400 depending on tank size.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: Nothing.
costs.fiveYear: Nil if stored properly; UV degrades outdoor-stored fabric, so keep it indoors between seasons unless it is rated for permanent exposure.

differentiators.label: Versus clearing 3 m around the tank
differentiators.detail: Clearing is free, more effective and required by most propane codes anyway. Do it first. The cover is a supplement to a cleared tank, not a substitute for clearing.

differentiators.label: Versus wetting the tank
differentiators.detail: Water cooling is what fire crews actually do and it works better — but it requires someone present with a hose. The cover works when nobody is home.

differentiators.label: The safety caveat that matters
differentiators.detail: Never fit anything that obstructs the pressure relief valve. A tank that cannot vent is a far worse problem than a tank that gets hot. If the cover's instructions are vague about the PRV, do not buy it.

differentiators.label: Check with your supplier
differentiators.detail: Some propane suppliers have views about aftermarket covers on leased tanks. A two-minute phone call avoids a dispute.

buying.lead: Days to two weeks
buying.where: Wildfire equipment suppliers, welding and industrial safety distributors, Amazon.
buying.note: Measure the tank first — diameter and length for horizontals, height for cylinders. Ask for the fabric's temperature rating in writing.

install.time: 10 minutes
install.note: Fit it, check the PRV is clear, secure the straps. Do it at the start of fire season and leave it if the fabric is UV-rated; otherwise fit it when risk rises.

ongoing.note: Inspect for UV damage and abrasion annually. Confirm the PRV is still unobstructed after any windstorm.

alternatives.name: A properly cleared 3 m radius around the tank
alternatives.note: Free, code-required, more effective. Non-negotiable regardless of whether you buy a cover.

alternatives.name: Relocating the tank away from the structure and the fuel
alternatives.note: The permanent fix, and worth pricing with your supplier if the tank sits in a bad spot.

guide.verdict: Cheap and sensible, but strictly a supplement. If the ground around your tank is not already cleared to bare mineral soil or gravel for 3 m, spend the Saturday before you spend the money.

name: Portable Gas Fire Pump (1.5 in)
pick: Best home fire pump
priceNote: Buy with a suction kit and foot valve
summary: A high-pressure 1.5 in gas pump moves water from a pool, pond or tank at enough pressure to run a roof sprinkler kit plus a hose line. The Honda-engine models are the reliability benchmark; buy the high-pressure variant, not the trash-pump variant.
pros: Independent of municipal water
Drives sprinklers and hose simultaneously
Also useful for flood pumping
cons: Gas storage and monthly test-runs required
Noisy; must run outdoors
bestFor: Any home with a pool, pond or storage tank.

guide.howItWorks: A petrol engine driving a centrifugal pump that draws water from a tank, pond, pool, creek or cistern and pushes it out at 1.5 inch fire-hose pressure. It is the component that makes every other water-based defence keep working after municipal pressure drops — which it reliably does during a major fire, when the whole neighbourhood is drawing at once and hydrants are being pumped by crews.
guide.market: Portable fire pumps split into three tiers. Agricultural and utility transfer pumps at CAD $400–$1,200 move volume at low pressure — fine for filling a tank, inadequate for sprinklers on a roof. Genuine light portable fire pumps — the Wick, Mark-3 and Honda-powered equivalents used by forestry crews — run CAD $2,500–$8,000 and deliver the pressure that actually pushes water uphill through hose to a roofline. Between them sit a growing number of CAD $1,000–$2,500 units marketed at homeowners, of variable honesty about their pressure curves. The specification that matters is not horsepower, it is the pump curve: pressure delivered at your required flow, at your elevation.

features.label: Pressure at flow
features.detail: The only number that matters. You want a curve, not a headline psi. Sprinklers on a two-storey roof need roughly 50–80 psi at the head after friction and elevation losses.

features.label: 1.5 in fire-hose fittings
features.detail: NPSH or NH threads, so it connects to real fire hose rather than garden hose. Adapters exist but every fitting costs you pressure.

features.label: Self-priming or foot-valve draft
features.detail: Determines how quickly you can start drawing from a static source and how much fuss the lift is.

features.label: Four-stroke engine
features.detail: Easier fuel, better starting after storage, and no mixing errors under stress. Two-strokes are lighter, which forestry crews care about and you do not.

features.label: Electric start on some models
features.detail: Worth having if anyone in the household will struggle with a pull cord.

costs.upfront: CAD $1,200–$8,000 / USD $900–$6,000. The honest homeowner band for something that will actually run roof sprinklers is CAD $2,500–$5,000.
costs.consumables: Fuel — CAD $20–$60 per hour of running for larger units. Oil, spark plug, impeller wear rings over time.
costs.ancillary: This is where budgets break. Hose and nozzle: CAD $500–$1,500. Suction hose and strainer: CAD $200–$500. Water source — a tank is CAD $2,000–$8,000. Fuel storage cans. A pump with nothing to draw from is furniture.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $400–$1,200 in service, fuel stabiliser and the annual test-run fuel. Budget a carburettor clean at least once.

differentiators.label: Versus relying on the municipal tap
differentiators.detail: The whole argument. In a significant interface fire, system pressure drops, sometimes to nothing, exactly when your sprinklers need it. A pump and a tank is the difference between a defence that runs and a defence that stops.

differentiators.label: Versus a transfer pump from the farm store
differentiators.detail: A CAD $600 transfer pump moves a lot of water at low pressure. It will fill a tank and it will not push water to a roofline through 30 m of hose. Check the curve, not the price.

differentiators.label: Versus a permanently installed system's pump
differentiators.detail: A portable can be moved, lent to a neighbour and taken to a second property. A fixed pump starts from your phone. Choose on whether you will be present.

differentiators.label: The neighbourhood angle
differentiators.detail: One good pump and 200 m of hose shared between four households is a common and sensible arrangement in rural BC and Alberta. It also means someone has to own the maintenance.

buying.lead: 2–8 weeks for serious units; longer in summer
buying.where: Forestry and firefighting equipment distributors, wildfire equipment specialists such as Flash Wildfire Services, and some rural equipment dealers. Not, generally, a big-box store.
buying.note: Take your numbers to the supplier: hose length, elevation from water source to highest sprinkler, number of heads and their flow rating. A dealer who cannot turn that into a pump recommendation with a curve is selling you a box.

install.time: Setup 20–40 minutes; siting and plumbing a permanent draft point, a day
install.note: Decide the pump's home now: a level, non-combustible pad near the water source, out of the weather, with the suction line short and the lift under about 5 m. A pump with a long, high suction lift will not prime when you need it and you will not have time to work out why.

ongoing.note: This is the highest-maintenance item on the site and the one most likely to fail from neglect. Run it monthly through fire season and at least quarterly otherwise. Use fuel stabiliser or drain the carburettor. Service annually. A pump that has sat untouched for eighteen months will not start on the day.

alternatives.name: A permanently installed pump as part of a Frontline-type system
alternatives.note: Starts remotely, costs far more, is somebody else's maintenance responsibility if you buy a service plan.

alternatives.name: A shared neighbourhood pump
alternatives.note: A quarter the cost each. Requires an agreement about storage, maintenance and who gets it first.

guide.verdict: If you are only going to spend serious money once in the water category, spend it here rather than on better sprinkler heads. And then accept that you have bought an engine, with everything that implies — the pump that fails is almost always the pump nobody started for a year.

name: 1.5 in Fire Hose & Fog Nozzle Kit
pick: Essential add-on
priceNote: 50 ft or 100 ft lengths; NH or camlock fittings
summary: Real fire hose with a fog/straight adjustable nozzle. Match the fitting thread to your pump (NH/NST in North America). Garden hose melts and kinks; this doesn't.
pros: Handles pump pressure
Fog pattern knocks down embers
Lays flat for storage
cons: Thread standards are confusing — check before buying
bestFor: Anyone buying a fire pump.

guide.howItWorks: Real 1.5 inch fire hose and a fog nozzle — the same equipment a wildland crew carries — connected to a pump. Fire hose is not big garden hose: it is designed to carry high pressure with low friction loss, which is what lets you move usable water 30–60 m to a roofline instead of losing all your pressure in the line.
guide.market: Hose is sold by forestry and firefighting supply distributors in standard 50 or 100 ft lengths, at CAD $150–$500 per length depending on construction. The market splits between single-jacket forestry hose — light, cheap, adequate for structure protection — and double-jacket municipal hose, heavier, tougher and roughly double the price. Nozzles range from a CAD $80 basic fog nozzle to CAD $600 for a professional adjustable-gallonage unit. For homeowner structure protection, single-jacket 1.5 in hose and a mid-range fog nozzle is the honest answer.

features.label: 1.5 in diameter
features.detail: The standard for structure protection. 1 in forestry hose is lighter but chokes the flow a serious pump can deliver.

features.label: Low friction loss
features.detail: The reason it is not garden hose. Fire hose delivers usable pressure at the far end of a long lay; garden hose does not.

features.label: Fog nozzle
features.detail: Adjustable from straight stream for reach to wide fog for heat protection and self-shielding. The fog pattern is a genuine safety feature, not a convenience.

features.label: Standard threads
features.detail: NPSH or NH — match your pump and match your neighbours if you may ever share. Mismatched threads are the classic day-of failure.

features.label: Storage
features.detail: Sold rolled or in a hose pack. It needs to be dried after use or it mildews.

costs.upfront: CAD $600–$2,000 for a practical kit — two to four 50 ft lengths, a nozzle, a gated wye and adapters.
costs.consumables: None, but gaskets perish and should be replaced every few years.
costs.ancillary: A pump. Without one this is decorative.
costs.fiveYear: CAD $100–$300 in gaskets and the odd replacement length. Well-stored hose lasts decades.

differentiators.label: Versus garden hose
differentiators.detail: At 30 m and 40 psi, garden hose has given up most of its pressure to friction. Fire hose has not. If you have gone to the expense of a pump, hooking it to garden hose throws away most of what you paid for.

differentiators.label: Single versus double jacket
differentiators.detail: Single is lighter, cheaper and easier for one person to move. Double survives being dragged over gravel and hot ground. For homeowner use, single-jacket is the sensible default.

differentiators.label: Thread compatibility
differentiators.detail: Check what your local fire department uses. If a crew arrives and can couple to your hose, that is worth something. If nobody's threads match, you have four separate private systems on one road.

differentiators.label: The physical reality
differentiators.detail: Charged 1.5 in hose is heavy and it kicks. One person can manage it; it is not effortless. Practise with water before you need to.

buying.lead: 2–6 weeks from distributors
buying.where: Forestry and firefighting supply houses, wildfire equipment specialists. Occasionally good used hose from fire department surplus — pressure-test it before trusting it.
buying.note: Buy the adapters at the same time as the hose. The most common story in this category is a complete kit that will not connect to the tap, the pump or the neighbour's line.

install.time: Setup 10–20 minutes for a typical lay
tools: A hose roller or just patience
install.note: Lay it out once, in the spring, along the route you would actually use. Note where it snags, where it crosses a driveway, and whether the length reaches the far corner. Store it where you can get it in the dark.

ongoing.note: Dry thoroughly after every use — wet hose rolled up mildews and rots. Check gaskets annually. Reroll differently each year so it does not take a permanent set.

alternatives.name: Heavy-duty garden hose and a firefighting-style nozzle
alternatives.note: A fraction of the cost, a fraction of the reach and pressure. Reasonable for a small lot with municipal pressure; wrong behind a real pump.

alternatives.name: Fixed sprinklers instead of a hose line
alternatives.note: Runs unattended. A hose needs a person, but goes exactly where the problem is.

guide.verdict: Buy it as part of the pump decision, never separately, and buy the adapters in the same order. The most expensive mistake here is a good pump joined to the house by garden hose.

name: Poly Water Storage Tank (1,000–2,500 gal)
pick: Water source
priceNote: Freight delivery; local dealers often cheaper
summary: If you don't have a pool, a dedicated poly tank is the practical way to guarantee water when the hydrants drop. Site it away from the house with a 1.5 in outlet and camlock fitting ready for your pump.
pros: Guarantees supply
Doubles for irrigation and outage water
cons: Bulky; freight cost
Needs a level pad and winterization in Canada
bestFor: Rural and acreage homes without a pool.

guide.howItWorks: A large polyethylene tank that holds the water your pump draws from. It is the least interesting item on this site and frequently the one that decides whether anything else works, because a sprinkler system with no independent supply stops the moment municipal pressure drops — which is precisely when you need it.
guide.market: Poly tanks are a commodity agricultural product sold in every rural region of North America, typically CAD $1.20–$3.00 per gallon of capacity for tanks between 1,000 and 5,000 gallons. Vertical tanks are cheapest per litre; low-profile and underground tanks cost more and are less obtrusive. The fire-specific considerations are few but real: UV-stabilised resin, a fitting arrangement that lets a pump draw properly, and siting that keeps the tank itself out of the fire. Nothing about this market is wildfire-branded and you should not pay a premium for anything that is.

features.label: Capacity
features.detail: Size it from run time, not from what fits. A full roofline of sprinklers uses roughly 1,200–2,500 L per hour — so two hours of protection is 2,500–5,000 L, and that is a modest goal.

features.label: UV-stabilised resin
features.detail: Non-negotiable for an outdoor tank. Non-stabilised poly chalks and cracks in a few seasons.

features.label: Bottom draw fitting
features.detail: A 2 in bulkhead fitting near the base so the pump can draw the whole volume rather than the top half.

features.label: Fill options
features.detail: Roof catchment, a well, a municipal fill, or a water-hauler visit. Most people use more than one.

features.label: Freeze management
features.detail: In most of Canada the tank drains for winter or is buried below frost. This is a design decision, not an afterthought.

costs.upfront: CAD $1,500–$6,000 / USD $1,200–$4,500 for 1,000–2,500 gallons, before site work.
costs.consumables: Water. Refilling a 2,500 gal tank from a hauler is CAD $150–$400 depending on distance.
costs.ancillary: The base is the hidden cost — a compacted gravel or concrete pad, CAD $500–$3,000. Plumbing, fittings and a fill line, CAD $300–$1,000. Delivery of a large tank to a rural address, CAD $200–$800.
costs.fiveYear: Minimal. Occasional fitting replacement and refills. A well-sited poly tank lasts 15–25 years.

differentiators.label: Versus a swimming pool
differentiators.detail: If you have a pool you already have 30,000–80,000 L and you need a pump and a strainer, not a tank. Pools are the most under-used wildfire water source in North America.

differentiators.label: Versus a pond or creek
differentiators.detail: Free and effectively unlimited, if you have one and it does not run dry in August. Needs a foot valve and a drafting setup, and needs the lift to be under about 5 m.

differentiators.label: Versus a cistern or buried tank
differentiators.detail: Buried tanks solve freezing and appearance and cost roughly double, plus excavation. Worth pricing if the tank would otherwise sit in the front yard.

differentiators.label: Siting
differentiators.detail: Put it uphill of the pump if you possibly can — a flooded suction beats a lift every time. Keep it clear of the fuel, and remember a poly tank is itself combustible when empty.

buying.lead: 1–6 weeks; large tanks are often a special order and freight is the constraint
buying.where: Farm and ranch supply, water-systems dealers, plastics distributors. Genuinely a rural commodity.
buying.note: Work out your required run time first and buy the capacity that gives you. Buying a tank because it was the one in the yard is how people end up with forty minutes of protection.

install.time: A day for the pad, half a day to set and plumb the tank
tools: Excavation or a compacted gravel pad
Help — large tanks are unwieldy even empty
install.note: The pad is the job. A 2,500 gal tank weighs about 9,500 kg full, so the base has to be level, compacted and full-footprint. A tank on an uneven base will crack at the seam within a couple of years.

ongoing.note: Keep it full through fire season — a tank at a third is a third of a defence. Drain or protect against freezing. Check fittings for weeps annually and clear debris from the fill screen.

alternatives.name: A swimming pool plus a strainer and foot valve
alternatives.note: Vastly more water for a few hundred dollars, if you already have the pool.

alternatives.name: A pond, creek or dugout with a drafting setup
alternatives.note: Free where available. Verify it still has water in a dry August, not in May.

alternatives.name: Multiple IBC totes
alternatives.note: CAD $150–$400 each for 1,000 L. Cheap, ugly, and a legitimate way to build storage incrementally.
