A 2025–2026 cost guide puts a small cookline at about USD $3,500–$7,000, mid-size at $7,000–$12,000 and large or multi-hood at $12,000–$25,000+.

features.label: Appliance-specific nozzles
features.detail: Each nozzle is placed for a particular appliance in a particular position. Move the fryer and the coverage no longer matches.

features.label: Fuel shut-off
features.detail: Discharge must cut gas or electric supply to the cooking line so the fire is not re-fed.

features.label: Release options
features.detail: Fusible-link mechanical release is the traditional design; pneumatic and electronic detection are offered by Amerex and others.

features.label: Water-assisted designs
features.detail: Ansul PIRANHA adds a water spray after the chemical for cooling.

features.label: Listed to UL 300 / ULC-ORD-C1254.6
features.detail: These are the key tests for restaurant systems. UL 300 replaced the older dry-chemical hood systems.

costs.upfront: Small cookline about USD $3,500–$7,000 (≈ CAD $4,800–$9,700); mid-size USD $7,000–$12,000 (≈ CAD $9,700–$16,600); large or multi-hood USD $12,000–$25,000+ (≈ CAD $16,600–$34,500+). Example: an Ansul R-102 on a 10 ft hood at about USD $10,400 for hardware and install, before permit and acceptance test.
costs.consumables: Fusible links replaced at least annually or semiannually per the manufacturer. Recharge after a discharge about USD $400–$900+ per hood.
costs.ancillary: Permit and acceptance test, gas shut-off valve, the Class K portable extinguisher, and hood and duct cleaning to NFPA 96.
costs.fiveYear: Ten semiannual inspections at about USD $200–$500 each — roughly USD $2,000–$5,000 — plus link replacements, hood and duct cleaning, and any recharge.

differentiators.label: Versus a Class K extinguisher alone
differentiators.detail: Not an option for commercial cooking that produces grease-laden vapours. The extinguisher is a backup, and the hood system must be activated first.

differentiators.label: Versus old dry-chemical hood systems
differentiators.detail: UL 300 replaced them. Wet chemical works on modern high-efficiency fryers that hold heat longer.

differentiators.label: Bundled with the hood
differentiators.detail: Kitchen ventilation contractors often supply the suppression system with the hood, which simplifies coordination but limits comparison shopping.

buying.lead: Days to a few weeks for design, permit and acceptance test
buying.where: Not sold to end users — through manufacturer-authorised, factory-trained distributors who design, install and service it (Ansul and Amerex distributor locators, Pyro-Chem and Kidde Fire Systems distributors). Often bundled with the hood by the kitchen ventilation contractor.
buying.note: Use the same company for install and semiannual service where possible; they will know your nozzle layout.

install.time: Typically a day or two on site, plus the acceptance test
install.note: Not legally or realistically an owner install. The fire official usually witnesses the acceptance test.

ongoing.note: Semiannual inspection by a certified technician under NFPA 17A/96, fusible links replaced on the manufacturer's schedule, and hood and duct cleaning at a frequency set by cooking volume under NFPA 96. Tell your service company before moving or adding appliances.

alternatives.name: Class K wet-chemical extinguisher
alternatives.note: Required as a backup, not a substitute.

alternatives.name: Water-assisted designs (e.g. Ansul PIRANHA)
alternatives.note: Add cooling after the chemical discharge; ask your distributor whether it suits your line.

guide.verdict: If you cook with grease commercially, this is not optional, and the main decisions are which distributor and which release type. Keep it inspected every six months, and treat every change to the cooking line as a call to your fire-system technician first.

standards.CA: The National Fire Code and National Building Code of Canada reference NFPA 96; systems listed to ULC-ORD-C1254.6.
standards.US: NFPA 96 requires automatic fire extinguishing for cooking that produces grease-laden vapours; systems installed to NFPA 17A and listed to UL 300.

guide.whoNeeds: Any commercial kitchen with cooking operations that produce grease-laden vapours — fryers, griddles, char-broilers and similar under a hood.
caveats: Any change to the cooking line — a new fryer or moved appliances — requires the system to be re-evaluated, because nozzle coverage is position-specific.
A Class K portable extinguisher is still required near the cooking line, and the hood system must be activated first.
The agent is a corrosive alkaline potassium salt solution; expect clean-up and possible equipment damage after a discharge.
Manufacturer pages we checked did not display the UL 300 / ULC listing; confirm the listing with your distributor.

sources.label: ThePricer — kitchen hood fire suppression system cost

guide.costNote: Installed-cost planning ranges from a US cost-guide site, 2025–2026. CAD figures are converted from USD at ~1.38; we found no Canadian contractor pricing source. Get at least two local distributor quotes.

name: Automatic Tube Suppression for Cabinets, CNC Machines and Panels
pick: Inside-the-box protection that needs no power
priceNote: Quote-only; no public price
summary: A pressurised polymer tube runs through the protected enclosure; heat from a fire bursts the tube and releases agent right at the source. It needs no electrical power to detect or discharge.
pros: Detects and discharges inside the enclosure, at the source of the fire
No power needed for activation
Choice of agents to suit the hazard, from clean agent to CO2 to Class D powder
cons: Protects only the enclosure; open-front machines need sealing to hold agent
Tube can be damaged by abrasion or chemicals
Quote-only pricing; ask for the specific UL/FM listing
bestFor: CNC machines, electrical panels, fume hoods, battery cabinets and wind turbine nacelles.

guide.howItWorks: A pressurised polymer detection tube is routed through the enclosure. When fire heats the tube, it softens and bursts at the hottest point. In a direct system, agent discharges straight out of that burst point. In an indirect system, the pressure drop opens a valve that sends agent to fixed nozzles. Agents include FK-5-1-12, CO2, dry chemical, Class D powder and nitrogen, chosen for the hazard. A pressure switch can signal an alarm panel or shut down the machine.
guide.market: Sold through manufacturer distributor networks — Firetrace offers a distributor portal and quote requests — with installation by trained distributors recommended; some units are also sold through industrial suppliers. Makers include Firetrace and Rotarex Firetec; Stat-X sells thermal aerosol units for cabinets. We found no public pricing.

features.label: Direct discharge
features.detail: Agent comes out of the burst point in the tube. Simple and suited to small enclosures.

features.label: Indirect discharge
features.detail: The tube acts as a detector and opens a valve feeding fixed nozzles. Better for larger volumes.

features.label: Agent choice
features.detail: FK-5-1-12, CO2, dry chemical, Class D powder or nitrogen, depending on the hazard.

features.label: Machine shutdown
features.detail: A pressure switch can signal an alarm panel or cut power to the machine.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get quotes. Firetrace prices on request.
costs.consumables: Agent and tube replacement after a discharge. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Alarm and shutdown wiring, and sealing work on open enclosures. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.fiveYear: Typically semiannual inspections. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus room-level sprinklers
differentiators.detail: A sprinkler responds once the room ceiling is hot. A tube system acts inside the cabinet, earlier, and can use an agent that does not harm electronics.

differentiators.label: Versus a portable extinguisher
differentiators.detail: Works unattended, including in machines running overnight.

differentiators.label: Versus aerosol units
differentiators.detail: Stat-X thermal units are self-contained aerosol generators for cabinets — a different technology for a similar job.

buying.lead: Quote and design by a distributor; varies
buying.where: Through manufacturer distributor networks (Firetrace distributor portal and quote requests; Stat-X distributors). Some units are sold through industrial suppliers, but installation by a trained distributor is recommended.
buying.note: Ask which third-party listings or approvals apply to the specific model and agent you are buying.

install.time: Hours per enclosure for simple systems
install.note: Route the tube away from moving parts, abrasion and chemicals.

ongoing.note: Typically semiannual inspection of pressure gauges and tube condition.

alternatives.name: Stat-X thermal aerosol units
alternatives.note: Self-contained units for cabinets and panels.

alternatives.name: Wet-pipe sprinkler system (NFPA 13)
alternatives.note: Room-level protection, but slower to react to a fire inside an enclosure and uses water.

guide.verdict: For a costly machine or panel where a fire would start inside a box, a tube system puts detection and agent exactly where it is needed. Get the listing details in writing, and seal the enclosure well enough to hold the agent.

standards.CA: Pre-engineered systems under the NFPA standard for the agent used (NFPA 2001 clean agent, NFPA 12 CO2, NFPA 17 dry chemical). Ask for the ULC listing.
standards.US: Pre-engineered systems under the NFPA standard for the agent used (NFPA 2001, NFPA 12, NFPA 17). Firetrace says its systems are tested and approved by third parties; ask for the specific UL/FM listing.

guide.whoNeeds: An owner or insurer choice for CNC machines, electrical panels, fume hoods, wind turbine nacelles and battery cabinets.
caveats: Protects only the enclosure; open-front machines need enclosures sealed enough to hold the agent.
The tube can be damaged by mechanical abrasion or chemicals.
Ask for the UL, ULC or FM listing that applies to each model and use.
guide.costNote: No public price was found; Firetrace and similar makers price on request.

name: Vehicle and Mobile Equipment Suppression
pick: Engine-bay protection for buses and heavy equipment
priceNote: Per-vehicle quote; no public price
summary: Engine-compartment systems for buses, trucks and mining, forestry and construction equipment detect fire and discharge water mist, dry chemical or a dual agent. Insurers and some jurisdictions require them on certain vehicles.
pros: Fogmaker systems need no power for activation or monitoring
Discharge continues cooling to help prevent re-ignition
Choice of water mist, dry chemical or dual-agent systems
cons: Must be installed by a certified installer for the function to be guaranteed
Requirements in Canada and the US vary and is not published
No public price
bestFor: Buses, mining and forestry machines, and construction equipment.

guide.howItWorks: Fogmaker uses a pressurised detection tube and a piston accumulator at 100–105 bar: when fire bursts the tube, the accumulator drives high-pressure water mist through nozzles in the engine bay, with no electrical power needed for activation or monitoring. AFEX and Ansul (CHECKFIRE) use dry chemical or dual-agent systems with linear or infrared detection. In each case discharge is designed to keep cooling after knock-down to prevent re-ignition from hot engine parts.
guide.market: Sold and installed only through certified distributors and authorised service technicians. Fogmaker states that guaranteed function requires a certified installer and operates in North America through Fogmaker USA. AFEX and Ansul vehicle systems serve mining, forestry and heavy equipment. We found no public pricing.

features.label: Water mist (Fogmaker)
features.detail: High-pressure mist cools and smothers. Fogmaker offers a PFAS-free liquid, Eco 1.

features.label: No power required (Fogmaker)
features.detail: Activation and monitoring are mechanical and pressure-based.

features.label: Dry chemical and dual agent (AFEX, Ansul)
features.detail: Dry chemical knocks fire down; dual-agent designs add a liquid for cooling.

features.label: Detection options
features.detail: Linear heat detection or infrared, depending on system.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get quotes per vehicle.
costs.consumables: Agent refill after a discharge. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Downtime for installation and service. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.fiveYear: Fogmaker requires annual controls plus 5-year and 10-year services. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Water mist versus dry chemical
differentiators.detail: Mist cools hot surfaces that cause re-ignition; dry chemical is fast at knock-down. Dual-agent systems try to do both.

differentiators.label: Check the fluid
differentiators.detail: Fogmaker's Eco 1 liquid is PFAS-free; earlier fluid formulations should be checked.

buying.lead: Depends on distributor and fleet size
buying.where: Not sold to end users for self-install — through certified distributors and authorised service technicians (Fogmaker, AFEX and Ansul dealer networks).
buying.note: Ask your insurer which systems it accepts before choosing.

install.time: No reliable public figure — ask the distributor
install.note: Fogmaker states that guaranteed function requires a certified installer.

ongoing.note: Fogmaker: annual controls plus 5-year and 10-year services. Follow the maker's schedule for AFEX and Ansul systems.

alternatives.name: Portable extinguishers on the vehicle
alternatives.note: Needed regardless, but rely on the operator noticing the fire and stopping safely.

alternatives.name: Automatic tube suppression
alternatives.note: Similar detection principle for fixed machinery rather than vehicles.

guide.verdict: For buses and heavy equipment, an engine-bay system is the realistic way to stop a fire the operator cannot see. Check what your insurer and jurisdiction require, buy through a certified installer, and confirm the fluid is PFAS-free.

standards.CA: Requirements vary by province and sector and is not published; mining equipment is often covered by insurer or occupational health and safety rules, and NFPA 122 addresses mining equipment.
standards.US: Requirements vary by state and sector and is not published; NFPA 122 addresses mining equipment. In Europe, buses fall under UNECE R107. Fogmaker publishes its certifications on its website.

guide.whoNeeds: Mining and forestry equipment operators (often under insurer or occupational health and safety rules), bus fleets, and owners of construction equipment.
caveats: Fogmaker offers a PFAS-free liquid (Eco 1); check the formulation of older fluids.
US and Canadian requirements for buses and equipment vary by province, state and sector; check with your insurer and regulator.
Ask the distributor for the certification that applies to your vehicle type; European bus approvals (UNECE R107) do not automatically carry over.
guide.costNote: No public price was found; vehicle systems are quoted per vehicle by certified distributors.

name: Class K Wet-Chemical Extinguisher for Commercial Kitchens
pick: The required backup to a hood system
priceNote: No published price — get dealer quotes
summary: A portable wet-chemical extinguisher required near commercial cooking appliances that use vegetable or animal oils. It is a backup to the hood suppression system, not a replacement.
pros: Fine spray saponifies hot cooking oil and cools it without splashing burning oil
Usually supplied and serviced by the same company that services the hood system
Wall-mounted; no installation work
cons: Only a backup — the hood system must be activated first
Five-year hydrostatic test required
bestFor: Commercial kitchens with deep-fat fryers and other cooking with vegetable or animal oils.

guide.howItWorks: The extinguisher holds a potassium acetate or citrate solution and discharges it as a fine spray, which keeps it from splashing burning oil. On contact with hot fat, the agent saponifies — forming a soapy layer that seals the surface — while the water content cools the oil below its re-ignition point. A placard near the extinguisher states that the hood system must be activated first; the portable unit is for what remains.
guide.market: Made by Amerex, Ansul and Badger among others, and sold through fire equipment dealers — usually the same company that services the hood system — and industrial suppliers. We found no verified price.

features.label: Fine spray nozzle
features.detail: Applies agent gently so burning oil does not splash.

features.label: Saponifying agent
features.detail: Potassium acetate/citrate turns hot fat into a soapy blanket and cools it.

features.label: Placarding
features.detail: Signage must state that the hood system is activated first.

features.label: Class K rating
features.detail: Tested for cooking-oil fires under UL 711 in the US and CAN/ULC-S508 in Canada.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get dealer quotes.
costs.consumables: Recharge after use. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Bracket and placard, usually supplied by the dealer.
costs.fiveYear: Annual servicing under NFPA 10 plus a five-year hydrostatic test. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus the hood system
differentiators.detail: The hood system is the primary protection. The Class K unit is the required backup.

differentiators.label: Versus ABC dry-chemical extinguishers
differentiators.detail: Dry chemical is not suited to deep-fat fryer fires; Class K is the rated type for cooking oils.

differentiators.label: Versus home kitchen units
differentiators.detail: For home kitchens, see our separate wet-chemical kitchen extinguisher entry; this one is about the commercial code requirement.

buying.lead: Usually in stock with fire equipment dealers
buying.where: Fire equipment dealers — usually the same company that services your hood system — and industrial suppliers (Amerex, Ansul, Badger).
buying.note: Buy it with the hood service contract so it gets inspected on the same visit.

install.time: Minutes
install.note: Mount within 30 ft (about 9 m) of the cooking appliances, with the placard.

ongoing.note: Monthly visual check by staff, annual service under NFPA 10, and a hydrostatic test every five years.

alternatives.name: Commercial kitchen hood wet-chemical system
alternatives.note: The required primary protection; the Class K unit backs it up.

alternatives.name: ABC dry-chemical extinguisher
alternatives.note: Not a substitute on fryer fires; keep one for the rest of the building.

guide.verdict: If you run a commercial kitchen with fryers, you need one within reach of the line, and your hood service company should already be supplying it. Train staff to pull the hood system first.

standards.CA: Fire rating to CAN/ULC-S508, with agent-specific construction standards (CAN/ULC-S554 for water-based agents); maintenance under NFPA 10 as referenced by the National Fire Code of Canada.
standards.US: Class K fire test in UL 711; agent-specific construction standards (UL 8 for water-based agents). NFPA 10/96 require a Class K unit within 30 ft of commercial cooking appliances using vegetable or animal oils.

guide.whoNeeds: Any commercial kitchen cooking with vegetable or animal oils — NFPA 10/96 require a Class K extinguisher within 30 ft (about 9 m) of the appliances.
caveats: A backup only; the hood suppression system must be activated first.
NFPA 10 sets placement (within 30 ft of the cooking appliance) and a five-year hydrostatic test for Class K units; confirm local amendments with your fire official.

sources.label: UL — fire extinguisher testing and certification

guide.costNote: No published price was found; the price band is a placement estimate — get quotes from a fire equipment dealer.

name: Clean Agent System: FK-5-1-12 (formerly 3M Novec 1230)
pick: The usual default for new server-room gas systems — check the agent source
priceNote: Low four figures for a small room; much more with detection and sealing
summary: A fluorinated ketone stored as a liquid that turns to vapour on discharge, floods a sealed room and puts the fire out mainly by absorbing heat. It leaves no residue, which is why it is used in server rooms, archives and control rooms.
pros: No residue — electronics and paper are not soaked or coated
Reaches design concentration in about 10 seconds
Designed to be safe for people at design concentration within NFPA 2001 safety margins
cons: 3M stopped making Novec 1230 when it exited PFAS manufacturing at the end of 2025; recharge agent must now come from another listed source
Only works if the room holds the gas — open doors or unsealed penetrations defeat it
A fluorinated chemical that broad PFAS definitions capture, so future rules could affect it
bestFor: Enclosed server rooms, data closets, archives and control rooms where water damage would be worse than the fire.

guide.howItWorks: Detectors wired to a releasing panel start a pre-discharge alarm and countdown. The panel shuts down HVAC, closes dampers, then opens the cylinder valves. The liquid agent vaporizes through the nozzles and reaches its design concentration — roughly 4–6% — in about 10 seconds. It extinguishes mainly by pulling heat out of the flame. The concentration then has to be held for a set soak time, which is why the room is tested for airtightness with a door-fan (room integrity) test.
guide.market: This is an engineered or pre-engineered installed system, not a product you buy. For years the agent was mostly 3M Novec 1230. 3M announced in December 2022 that it would exit all PFAS manufacturing and says it completed that exit at the end of 2025. The chemical itself, FK-5-1-12, is still supplied by others: Fike sells SF 1230 through Standard Fluids (marketed as a drop-in), Kidde sells Fluoro-K and ANSUL sells SAPPHIRE. Janus Fire Systems and Firetrace also build FK-5-1-12 systems.

features.label: Total flooding
features.detail: The whole enclosure is brought to concentration, so the fire is reached wherever it is inside the room — including under raised floors if they are part of the protected volume.

features.label: Pre-discharge sequence
features.detail: Alarm, countdown, HVAC shutdown and damper closure happen before release, giving people time to leave and keeping the agent in the room.

features.label: No residue
features.detail: The agent evaporates, so there is no water or powder cleanup on the equipment.

features.label: Room integrity testing
features.detail: A door-fan test checks whether the room will hold concentration for the required soak time. It is re-evaluated annually under NFPA 2001.

costs.upfront: USD $2–$10 per sq ft protected (≈ CAD $2.75–$13.80). The source's example small server room of 500 sq ft came in at USD $2,000–$4,000; that is a low-end example, not a typical project with full detection and sealing.
costs.consumables: Recharge after a discharge roughly USD $12–$15 per lb of agent.
costs.ancillary: Room sealing, HVAC dampers and shutdowns, the releasing panel tie-in to the building alarm, and the integrity test. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.fiveYear: Semiannual and annual service visits under NFPA 2001. No reliable public figure for service contracts — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus HFC-227ea (FM-200)
differentiators.detail: Same total-flooding method. FK-5-1-12 is not an HFC, so it sits outside the US AIM Act HFC phase-down that is tightening FM-200 supply.

differentiators.label: Versus inert gas
differentiators.detail: Halocarbon systems need far fewer cylinders and no large pressure-relief vents. Inert gas avoids fluorinated chemicals altogether.

differentiators.label: Versus pre-action sprinklers
differentiators.detail: Often used instead of, or alongside, pre-action sprinklers. The gas protects the equipment without water; sprinklers protect the building if the gas cannot hold.

buying.lead: Design, room testing and installation; weeks for a typical room
buying.where: Not sold to end users — designed, installed, room-tested and serviced by each manufacturer's authorized, factory-trained special-hazard distributors.
buying.note: Ask which FK-5-1-12 source the distributor will use for the fill and future recharges, and confirm that source is listed with the system hardware being installed.

install.time: Days on site, after design and room sealing
install.note: The cylinders and pipe are the easy part. Sealing cable and pipe penetrations, fitting dampers and passing the door-fan test is where projects slip.

ongoing.note: NFPA 2001 calls for a semiannual check of agent quantity and pressure, an annual inspection and test, and an annual re-evaluation of room integrity. Cylinder hydrostatic test intervals follow DOT (US) or Transport Canada rules. Any new cable run through a wall can quietly break the room seal.

alternatives.name: Inert gas (Inergen, Argonite, nitrogen)
alternatives.note: No PFAS or HFC exposure, at the cost of many more cylinders and pressure-relief venting.

alternatives.name: Water mist
alternatives.note: Far less water than sprinklers and no chemical agent, but listings are hazard-specific.

alternatives.name: Pre-action sprinklers
alternatives.note: Keeps pipes dry until detection confirms a fire. Common alongside, or instead of, a gas system.

guide.verdict: Still a sound choice for a sealed room full of equipment that water would ruin. The Novec name is gone, not the agent: get the system from an authorized distributor, make sure the recharge agent is listed with your hardware, and budget for keeping the room airtight year after year.

standards.CA: Designed to NFPA 2001; the alarm interface also falls under CAN/ULC-S524. Use ULC-listed system hardware.
standards.US: Designed to NFPA 2001; systems listed to UL 2166 (halocarbon systems) and FM Approved. NFPA 2001 and FM Data Sheet 4-9 treat FK-5-1-12 generically, but each manufacturer's hardware is listed only with specific agent sources.

guide.whoNeeds: Usually an owner or insurer choice rather than a code requirement. It makes sense for enclosed rooms of high-value or business-critical equipment where downtime or water damage would cost more than the system.
caveats: 3M announced in December 2022 that it would exit all PFAS manufacturing and states it completed that exit at the end of 2025. Novec 1230 is no longer made by 3M.

FK-5-1-12 is still supplied by others (Fike SF 1230 via Standard Fluids, Kidde Fluoro-K, ANSUL SAPPHIRE). For a recharge, confirm the agent source is listed with your system's hardware — listings are not interchangeable.
FK-5-1-12 is a fluorinated chemical captured by broad PFAS definitions. We could not confirm whether any US state or Canadian rule currently targets it, but future PFAS restrictions could.
It only works in an enclosure that holds concentration. Open doors, unsealed penetrations or a failed integrity test defeat it.

sources.label: Safe and Sound — fire suppression system cost

guide.costNote: Planning ranges from a US contractor cost guide (getsafeandsound.com), 2025–2026; CAD figures converted from USD at ~1.38 because we found no Canadian source. Real projects with detection, room sealing and integrity testing often exceed the small-room example. Get at least two local quotes.

name: Clean Agent System: HFC-227ea (FM-200 and equivalents)
pick: Huge installed base, shrinking future
priceNote: Similar to other clean agents; recharge supply is tightening in the US
summary: The most widely installed halocarbon clean agent of the past 25 years, used in server and control rooms. It is an HFC, so in the US it falls under the AIM Act phase-down and new rules requiring recycled agent.
pros: Proven, well-understood total-flooding agent with a large service network
No residue on equipment
Discharges to design concentration in about 10 seconds
cons: US servicing must use recycled HFCs from January 1, 2026; new US installations must use recycled HFCs from January 1, 2030
Virgin supply is shrinking because fire suppression lost its AIM Act allowance carve-out (outside aerospace and mission-critical military)
Needs a sealed room, like every total-flooding gas
bestFor: Existing server and control rooms already protected by FM-200 that need to be maintained, rather than new rooms.

guide.howItWorks: The same total-flooding approach as FK-5-1-12: detectors trigger an alarm and countdown, the panel shuts HVAC and releases agent from pressurized cylinders, and the room reaches design concentration in about 10 seconds. The agent puts the fire out mainly by absorbing heat, and the room has to hold that concentration for a set time. Nothing is left behind afterwards.
guide.market: Sold and serviced only through authorized distributors and installers. FM-200 is Chemours' brand name for the agent; Kidde, Fike and Janus build systems around HFC-227ea. The existing installed base is large, but new installations increasingly use FK-5-1-12 or inert gas. In the US, the rules governing HFCs have changed what owning one of these systems involves.

features.label: Total flooding
features.detail: Fills the whole enclosure, reaching fires inside cabinets and under raised floors that are within the protected volume.

features.label: 10-second discharge
features.detail: Fast enough to stop a fire before it spreads through equipment.

features.label: Residue-free
features.detail: Equipment can usually be brought back into service without cleanup of the agent itself.

features.label: Large service base
features.detail: Decades of installations mean many technicians know the hardware — though in the US they now need specific training (see below).

costs.upfront: USD $2–$10 per sq ft protected (≈ CAD $2.75–$13.80). The source's example 500 sq ft FM-200 room was USD $2,000–$4,000.
costs.consumables: Recharge roughly USD $12–$15 per lb. In the US, servicing must now use recycled HFC, so expect supply and price to track the phase-down.
costs.ancillary: Room sealing, dampers, alarm integration and integrity testing. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.fiveYear: Semiannual and annual NFPA 2001 service. No reliable public figure for service contracts — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus FK-5-1-12
differentiators.detail: Same job, same room requirements. FK-5-1-12 is not an HFC, so it is outside the AIM Act phase-down; it has its own PFAS-related questions instead.

differentiators.label: Versus inert gas
differentiators.detail: Inert gas uses no synthetic agent but needs far more cylinder space and pressure-relief venting.

differentiators.label: What the US rules do and do not say
differentiators.detail: EPA's Technology Transitions page does not list fire suppression as a restricted sector, so existing systems are not banned. The pressure is on supply: recycled agent for servicing now, and for new installs from 2030.

buying.lead: Weeks for design, installation and room testing
buying.where: Not sold to end users — through authorized special-hazard distributors and installers only.
buying.note: For an existing system, ask your service company how it sources recycled HFC-227ea and what a full recharge would cost today. For a new room, ask for an FK-5-1-12 or inert gas quote alongside.

install.time: Days on site, after design and room sealing
install.note: As with any total-flooding gas, the room integrity work matters as much as the cylinders and piping.

ongoing.note: Same NFPA 2001 regime as FK-5-1-12: semiannual agent and pressure checks, annual inspection and test, annual room integrity review. In the US, technicians servicing HFC fire suppression equipment must be trained under the EPA Emissions Reduction and Reclamation rule by June 1, 2026, and releases must be minimized.

alternatives.name: FK-5-1-12 clean agent
alternatives.note: The usual replacement for new halocarbon systems.

alternatives.name: Inert gas (Inergen, Argonite, nitrogen)
alternatives.note: No synthetic agent; bigger footprint.

alternatives.name: Pre-action sprinklers
alternatives.note: Water-based protection that keeps pipes dry until a fire is confirmed.

guide.verdict: If you already have an FM-200 system, keep it maintained — it still works and is not banned. If you are specifying a new room, especially in the US, the HFC phase-down makes this the harder choice to support over the system's life; get FK-5-1-12 and inert gas quotes as well.

standards.CA: Designed to NFPA 2001 with ULC-listed hardware. Ask your distributor how Canadian HFC rules affect recharge supply.
standards.US: Designed to NFPA 2001; systems UL 2166 / FM listed. HFC handling under the EPA Emissions Reduction and Reclamation rule (40 CFR 84 subpart C) and the AIM Act allowance program.

guide.whoNeeds: An owner or insurer choice under NFPA 2001, not usually a code mandate. Mainly relevant today to owners of the many existing systems.
caveats: US EPA Emissions Reduction and Reclamation rule (40 CFR 84 subpart C): from January 1, 2026, servicing and repair of HFC fire suppression equipment must use recycled HFCs and releases must be minimized; from January 1, 2030, initial installation must use recycled HFCs.

Fire suppression (other than onboard aerospace and mission-critical military uses) is not among the AIM Act application-specific allowance uses renewed through 2030, so virgin HFC-227ea supply is shrinking under the phase-down.
EPA's Technology Transitions rules do not list fire suppression as a restricted sector, so existing systems are not prohibited.
We could not confirm Canadian HFC rules for fire suppression; do not assume the US dates apply in Canada.

sources.label: US EPA — Emissions Reduction and Reclamation fact sheet
International Fire & Safety Journal — EPA finalises fire suppression rule for HFC allowances
US EPA — Technology Transitions regulatory actions
Safe and Sound — fire suppression system cost

guide.costNote: Planning ranges from a US contractor cost guide (getsafeandsound.com), 2025–2026; CAD figures converted from USD at ~1.38 because we found no Canadian source. Real projects with detection, room sealing and integrity testing often exceed the small-room example. Get at least two local quotes.

name: Inert Gas Systems (IG-541 Inergen, IG-55 Argonite, IG-100 Nitrogen)
pick: The no-chemical-question clean agent
priceNote: No reliable public figure; more cylinders and space than halocarbons
summary: Blends of naturally occurring gases — nitrogen, argon and CO2 — flood a room and lower oxygen to a level that stops combustion but stays survivable for short exposure. There is no PFAS or HFC involved.
pros: No PFAS or HFC — unaffected by 3M's exit or the HFC phase-down
Leaves no residue
IG-541 includes about 8% CO2 to stimulate breathing in the reduced-oxygen atmosphere
cons: Needs significant floor space for high-pressure cylinders
Rooms need pressure-relief vents because of the large volume of gas
Refilling 300-bar cylinders is a logistics job, usually handled through manufacturer exchange programs
bestFor: Data centres, archives, telecom rooms and control rooms where the owner wants a gas system without synthetic agents and has room for the cylinders.

guide.howItWorks: Gas is stored in high-pressure cylinders, often 200–300 bar. On release it passes through pressure-reducing orifices and discharges over about 60 seconds, bringing the room's oxygen from 21% down to roughly 12–14%. That is too little for most fires to keep burning but, for a short exposure, survivable for people. IG-541 (Inergen) adds about 8% CO2 so that occupants breathe more deeply. Because so much gas enters the room, a pressure-relief vent is needed to stop walls and doors being damaged.
guide.market: Installed systems sold through authorized distributors and installers. ANSUL makes INERGEN (IG-541), KiddeFenwal markets NATURA inert gas systems, Firetrace makes CoolGen nitrogen systems and Fike also supplies inert gas. Interest has grown as halocarbon agents face PFAS and HFC pressure.

features.label: Natural gases only
features.detail: Nitrogen, argon and CO2 in various blends. Nothing to phase down or reformulate.

features.label: 60-second discharge
features.detail: Slower than the roughly 10 seconds for halocarbons, by design, to manage the large gas volume.

features.label: Oxygen reduction, not chemistry
features.detail: It works by lowering oxygen rather than by absorbing heat or chemical interference.

features.label: Cylinder exchange
features.detail: Manufacturers run exchange programs because refilling 300-bar cylinders on site is not practical.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get quotes. Expect more cylinders and floor space than an equivalent halocarbon system.
costs.consumables: Cylinder exchange after discharge. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Pressure-relief vents, room sealing, cylinder storage space and alarm integration.
costs.fiveYear: Semiannual pressure checks and annual inspection under NFPA 2001, plus cylinder hydrotests at their intervals. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus halocarbon clean agents
differentiators.detail: Avoids the 3M/PFAS and HFC phase-down issues entirely. The trade-off is footprint: many more cylinders and a vent in the room.

differentiators.label: Versus CO2 total flooding
differentiators.detail: CO2 systems raise CO2 to lethal levels. Inert gas systems are designed so the reduced-oxygen atmosphere is survivable for short exposure and can be used in occupied rooms.

buying.lead: Weeks for design, venting and installation
buying.where: Not sold to end users — designed and installed by authorized special-hazard distributors.
buying.note: Ask early where the cylinders will go and how the relief vent will be routed; those two questions decide whether inert gas fits the building.

install.time: Days on site, after design
install.note: The pressure-relief vent is a wall penetration that has to be planned with the building owner.

ongoing.note: NFPA 2001 semiannual pressure checks, annual inspection, room integrity checks and cylinder hydrostatic testing at the required intervals.

alternatives.name: FK-5-1-12 clean agent
alternatives.note: Smaller footprint and faster discharge; a fluorinated agent with supply-source questions since 3M's exit.

alternatives.name: Water mist
alternatives.note: Little water and no chemical agent, but listings are hazard-specific.

alternatives.name: Pre-action sprinklers
alternatives.note: The water-based option for the same rooms.

guide.verdict: The cleanest answer to the chemical questions hanging over halocarbon agents, if you have the space for the cylinders and can vent the room. We could not find a credible public cost figure, so compare it on real quotes against an FK-5-1-12 system.

standards.CA: Designed to NFPA 2001 with ULC-listed system hardware.
standards.US: Designed to NFPA 2001; systems UL listed and FM Approved.

guide.whoNeeds: Data centres, archives, telecom and control rooms where an owner or insurer wants a gas system — usually not a code requirement.
caveats: Refilling 300-bar cylinders is a logistics issue; plan on the manufacturer's exchange program after any discharge.
Needs significant cylinder storage space and pressure-relief vents in the protected room.
We found no reliable public cost figures for inert gas systems in North America.
guide.costNote: We found no reliable public cost source for inert gas systems in Canada or the US, so no figures are given. Get at least two local quotes, ideally alongside a halocarbon quote for the same room.

name: Water Mist Systems (e.g. Marioff HI-FOG)
pick: Sprinkler-style protection with a fraction of the water
priceNote: Engineered project; no reliable North American figure
summary: High-pressure systems turn water into very fine droplets that cool the fire and displace oxygen, using far less water than sprinklers. They are used in heritage buildings, data centres, hotels, turbine enclosures and ships.
pros: Much less water than sprinklers, so less water damage
Small-bore stainless tubing is easier to route through historic or finished buildings
No chemical agent and nothing to phase out
cons: Listings are application-specific — a design tested for a turbine enclosure does not transfer to a warehouse
Stainless components and water quality requirements raise component cost
Acceptance as a sprinkler alternative depends on the local authority having jurisdiction
bestFor: Heritage buildings, hotels, data centres and machinery or turbine enclosures where water damage, weight or retrofit disruption rule out ordinary sprinklers.

guide.howItWorks: Pumps or gas-driven cylinders push water at high pressure through micro-nozzles. The droplets are so small that they evaporate quickly, absorbing heat and locally reducing oxygen around the fire. Systems are either automatic-nozzle (each nozzle opens with heat, like a sprinkler) or open-nozzle deluge (all nozzles in a zone discharge together). Each design has to match a fire test protocol for the specific hazard.
guide.market: Engineered by the manufacturer or its certified integrators rather than sold as a product. Marioff (HI-FOG) is the best-known name; Fike also supplies water mist, and Victaulic makes the Vortex hybrid system. We found no reliable North American cost data; one UK trade article claimed lower capital cost than clean agent, but the source was too weak to use.

features.label: Fine droplets
features.detail: Large surface area means fast heat absorption with little water.

features.label: Small-bore stainless tubing
features.detail: Easier to thread through historic interiors and finished spaces than sprinkler pipe.

features.label: Automatic or deluge
features.detail: Sprinkler-like heads for rooms; open nozzles for machinery and enclosures.

features.label: Hazard-specific listings
features.detail: Every application must match a tested design — there is no general-purpose listing.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.consumables: Water. Gas-driven systems also need cylinder replacement after discharge.
costs.ancillary: Pump unit or cylinder bank, water supply and water quality treatment.
costs.fiveYear: NFPA 750 inspection and testing; Marioff offers lifecycle and maintenance programs. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus sprinklers
differentiators.detail: Far less water and lighter piping, at higher component cost. Whether it can replace required sprinklers is the local authority's call.

differentiators.label: Versus clean agent gas
differentiators.detail: Does not need a sealed room to hold concentration and has no PFAS or HFC questions, but it is water — not ideal directly on energized equipment unless the design is listed for it.

buying.lead: Engineering and approvals add weeks to months
buying.where: Not sold to end users — engineered and installed by the manufacturer or its certified integrators.
buying.note: Ask which tested design and listing the proposal relies on, and confirm with your local authority early if the system is meant to replace sprinklers.

install.time: Project-dependent; days to weeks
install.note: The small tubing is the advantage in retrofits — less demolition in finished or heritage spaces.

ongoing.note: Inspection and testing to NFPA 750. Water quality and stainless components matter, so follow the manufacturer's maintenance program.

alternatives.name: Wet or pre-action sprinklers
alternatives.note: The standard, cheaper-per-head option where water quantity is acceptable.

alternatives.name: Clean agent gas
alternatives.note: For sealed rooms of electronics.

alternatives.name: Inert gas
alternatives.note: Gas protection with no synthetic agent.

guide.verdict: A strong option where sprinkler water or pipework would do real harm — a heritage interior, a hotel retrofit, a turbine enclosure. It is an engineered, hazard-specific system: make sure the listing matches your hazard and that the local authority accepts it before you commit.

standards.CA: NFPA 750 design. Acceptance as a sprinkler alternative depends on the local authority having jurisdiction. Ask for ULC-listed components.
standards.US: NFPA 750 design; hazard-specific listings under FM Approvals (FM 5560) and UL 2167. Acceptance as a sprinkler alternative depends on the AHJ.

guide.whoNeeds: Buildings where water damage, structural weight or retrofit disruption make sprinklers or gas a poor fit; acceptance as a substitute for required sprinklers is decided locally.
caveats: Listings are application-specific; a design tested for a turbine enclosure doesn't transfer to a warehouse.
Water quality and stainless components matter, and component cost is higher than sprinkler pipe.
We found no reliable North American cost figures.
guide.costNote: We found no reliable North American cost source for water mist systems, so no figures are given. Get at least two local quotes against a sprinkler or clean-agent alternative for the same space.

name: Condensed Aerosol Generators (Stat-X, FirePro)
pick: Simple fixed protection for cabinets and enclosures
priceNote: No reliable public price — quoted per enclosure
summary: Unpressurized canisters hold a solid compound that, when triggered, releases a fine potassium-salt aerosol that interrupts the fire's chemical chain reaction. They are used for electrical cabinets, engine and generator enclosures and battery rooms.
pros: No piping and no pressure vessels — units mount directly in the space
Stat-X units are UL and ULC listed
FirePro cites a 15-year generator life with low maintenance
cons: Leaves a fine potassium-compound powder residue that needs cleanup — not 'clean' in the NFPA 2001 sense
Generators get hot when discharging and need clearance from combustibles and people
Visibility drops sharply during discharge
bestFor: Electrical cabinets, engine and generator enclosures and battery rooms that are normally unoccupied or have limited occupancy.

guide.howItWorks: An electrical signal from a detection panel or a thermal trigger ignites the solid compound inside the generator. The reaction releases micron-sized particles and gas that fill the enclosure and chemically quench the flames by interrupting the combustion chain reaction. Because nothing is stored under pressure there are no cylinders or pipes; the generators bolt into the protected space. NFPA 2010 covers these systems for enclosed volumes.
guide.market: Sold through distributor networks, not retail. Stat-X (made by Fireaway) reports 329 distributors in 94 countries; FirePro has a global distribution network and Firetrace distributes FirePro. Pricing is quoted per enclosure and we found no reliable public figure.

features.label: Unpressurized
features.detail: No cylinders to hydrotest and no pressure to lose over time.

features.label: No piping
features.detail: Each generator mounts in the space it protects, which suits cabinets and engine enclosures.

features.label: Chemical flame inhibition
features.detail: Works by interrupting the chain reaction rather than by cooling or oxygen reduction.

features.label: Hazardous-location listings
features.detail: Stat-X lists UL Class I Div 2, EN 15276 and IECEx/ATEX approvals in addition to UL/ULC.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.consumables: A discharged generator is replaced. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Detection and releasing panel if electrically triggered; cleanup of residue after a discharge.
costs.fiveYear: Periodic inspection of units and releasing circuits under NFPA 2010. FirePro cites a 15-year generator life.

differentiators.label: Versus clean agent gas
differentiators.detail: No cylinders, piping or room-integrity work, which makes it practical for small enclosures. The trade-off is a powder residue and reduced visibility.

differentiators.label: Versus dry chemical systems
differentiators.detail: Both leave powder. Aerosol generators are unpressurized and need no piping network.

differentiators.label: Occupancy
differentiators.detail: Designed for normally unoccupied or limited-occupancy spaces. FirePro says EPA SNAP lists its agent for normally occupied areas; check the specific product's listing for your use.

buying.lead: Depends on distributor and enclosure count
buying.where: Not typical retail — through Stat-X and FirePro distributor networks (Firetrace distributes FirePro).
buying.note: Ask for the listing that covers your specific enclosure type, and how the residue is cleaned up after a discharge.

install.time: Hours to days, depending on enclosure count and detection
install.note: Mounting is simple; the care goes into clearances, because the generators get hot during discharge.

ongoing.note: Periodic inspection of the generators and releasing circuits under NFPA 2010. No pressure gauges to watch.

alternatives.name: FK-5-1-12 clean agent
alternatives.note: No residue, but needs cylinders, piping and a sealed room.

alternatives.name: Pre-engineered dry chemical
alternatives.note: Common for process hazards; also leaves powder.

alternatives.name: Inert gas
alternatives.note: Residue-free with no synthetic agent, at a larger footprint.

guide.verdict: A practical way to protect a cabinet, engine bay or small battery room without cylinders or pipe. Go in knowing the space will be full of powder and smoke-like aerosol after a discharge, and keep it to spaces where that is acceptable.

standards.CA: ULC listed (Stat-X: EX 15004, 'Fixed Condensed Aerosol Extinguishing System Units'; FirePro shows ULC listing). Design under NFPA 2010.
standards.US: UL listed (Stat-X: EX 15004; FirePro shows UL listing); Stat-X also UL Class I Div 2. Design under NFPA 2010. FirePro states EPA SNAP lists its agent for normally occupied areas. We could not confirm a UL 2775 listing from either maker's page.

guide.whoNeeds: An owner or insurer choice under NFPA 2010 (Fixed Aerosol Fire-Extinguishing Systems), typically for enclosed equipment spaces.
caveats: Discharge leaves a fine potassium-compound powder residue; this is not a clean agent in the NFPA 2001 sense and cleanup is needed.
Generators get hot when discharging; clearance to combustibles and people is required.
Visibility drops sharply during discharge.
We found no reliable public price figures.
guide.costNote: We found no reliable public price source for aerosol generators in Canada or the US, so no figures are given. Get at least two distributor quotes for your enclosures.

name: Foam Fire Suppression Systems (Fixed Foam / Foam-Water)
pick: Essential for flammable liquids — and mid-transition away from PFAS
priceNote: USD $5–$20 per sq ft before any AFFF conversion work
summary: Foam concentrate mixed into water forms a blanket over burning flammable liquids, smothering and cooling the fire. It is used at fuel storage, aircraft hangars, refineries and chemical warehouses.
pros: Puts out flammable-liquid fires that water alone spreads
Can be delivered several ways: foam-water sprinklers, monitors, tank foam chambers or high-expansion generators
Fluorine-free (SFF/F3) concentrates are now available from the major makers
cons: Legacy fluorinated AFFF is being banned in Canada and in about 29 US states
Switching to fluorine-free foam usually means system cleaning and possibly redesign; residual PFAS in piping is a problem
Concentrate must be sample-tested annually
bestFor: Fuel storage and dispensing, aircraft hangars, refineries and chemical or flammable-liquid warehouses.

guide.howItWorks: A proportioner meters foam concentrate — typically 1–6% — into the water stream. The resulting foam is delivered by foam-water sprinklers, fixed monitors, foam chambers on storage tanks, or high-expansion generators that fill a space such as a hangar. The foam floats on the burning liquid, cutting off oxygen and vapour and cooling the surface. Older systems used fluorinated AFFF; new systems use fluorine-free foams (SFF or F3), which often need different hardware and higher application rates.
guide.market: Designed and installed by specialty fire-protection engineering contractors and foam distributors. ANSUL and Chemguard (both Johnson Controls) and National Foam are major makers of concentrates and hardware. The market is in the middle of a forced shift from PFAS-containing AFFF to fluorine-free foam on both sides of the border, with different timelines in Canada and in each US state.

features.label: Proportioning
features.detail: Meters concentrate into water at a set ratio, typically 1–6%.

features.label: Multiple delivery methods
features.detail: Foam-water sprinklers (NFPA 16), monitors, tank foam chambers, and low-, medium- or high-expansion generators (NFPA 11).

features.label: Fluorine-free concentrates
features.detail: SFF/F3 foams replace AFFF, but they are not drop-in: hardware and application rates often change.

features.label: Concentrate testing
features.detail: Foam concentrate degrades and is sample-tested annually.

costs.consumables: Foam concentrate replacement after discharge or failed testing. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: For existing AFFF systems: cleaning, possible redesign and disposal of PFAS-containing concentrate when converting. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.fiveYear: Annual concentrate sampling and NFPA 25/11 system tests. No reliable public figure — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus sprinklers alone
differentiators.detail: Plain water on a flammable-liquid fire can spread it. Foam is what makes a sprinkler or monitor system work on these hazards.

differentiators.label: AFFF versus fluorine-free
differentiators.detail: AFFF is being regulated out. Fluorine-free foam avoids PFAS liability but often needs different hardware and application rates — budget for engineering, not just a concentrate swap.

differentiators.label: Canada and US differ
differentiators.detail: Canada regulates AFFF federally on a fixed timeline; in the US it is a patchwork of state laws. Check the rules where the system actually is.

buying.lead: Engineering, approvals and installation; months for larger facilities
buying.where: Not sold to end users — through specialty fire-protection engineering contractors and foam distributors.
buying.note: If you have an existing AFFF system, ask for a transition plan: what concentrate is in it, which deadline applies to you, and what cleaning and redesign a fluorine-free conversion would involve.

install.time: Weeks for a facility system
install.note: Conversions are often harder than new installs because PFAS residue clings to existing piping and tanks.

ongoing.note: Annual foam concentrate sample testing and system tests under NFPA 25 and NFPA 11. Keep records of which concentrate is in the system — regulators and insurers will ask.

alternatives.name: Pre-engineered dry chemical
alternatives.note: Used on fuel dispensing and some process hazards; a different tool for smaller areas.

alternatives.name: Design and containment changes
alternatives.note: Drainage, diking and separation reduce how much foam protection a flammable-liquid area needs — a question for the fire protection engineer.

guide.verdict: If you store or handle flammable liquids at scale, foam is often the only fixed protection that works. For new systems, specify fluorine-free. For existing AFFF systems, start the conversion conversation now — the Canadian deadlines and many US state bans are fixed, and cleaning out PFAS takes longer than ordering new concentrate.

standards.CA: Design commonly to NFPA 11 and NFPA 16; ask for ULC-listed components. Federally, PFOS-based AFFF has been banned since 2013 and PFOA/long-chain (C8) AFFF is being phased out under CEPA (dates in caveats).
standards.US: NFPA 11 (low, medium and high expansion foam), NFPA 16 (foam-water sprinklers), NFPA 409 for aircraft hangars; concentrates and hardware UL 162 listed and FM Approved. PFAS foam restrictions are set state by state.

guide.whoNeeds: Facilities with flammable-liquid hazards — fuel storage, hangars (NFPA 409), refineries, chemical warehouses — where codes, insurers or the AHJ require foam protection.
caveats: US: about 29 states had enacted restrictions on PFAS Class B foam as of November 2025 — for example an Illinois manufacture and sale ban from January 1, 2025, and a New Mexico sales ban from January 1, 2027.

Canada: PFOS AFFF banned since 2013. C8 (PFOA/LC-PFCA) AFFF: import banned and use restricted from June 30, 2026; sales fully banned July 1, 2028; all use banned January 1, 2031. C6 AFFF is not yet prohibited — consultation closed November 25, 2025, with further consultation planned for spring 2027.
Changing to fluorine-free foam usually requires system cleaning and possibly redesign; residual PFAS in piping is a known problem.

guide.costNote: Per-square-foot range from a US contractor cost guide (getsafeandsound.com), 2025–2026; CAD figures converted from USD at ~1.38 because we found no Canadian source. AFFF conversion costs are not included. Get at least two local quotes.

name: Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Total Flooding and Local Application Systems
pick: Effective and residue-free — and lethal to anyone inside
priceNote: USD $20,000–$100,000+ per project
summary: High- or low-pressure CO2 floods an enclosure or blankets a single machine, smothering the fire. It leaves no residue but is lethal at the concentrations used, so it belongs only in normally unoccupied spaces.
pros: Residue-free, like the clean agents
Local application can protect a single machine such as a printing press or dip tank
CO2 is not a PFAS or HFC agent
cons: Fatal to people at total-flooding design concentrations
Requires lockout valves, odorizers and warning signage
Not recommended for occupied spaces
bestFor: Normally unoccupied machinery spaces, vaults and industrial process hazards such as printing presses and dip tanks.

guide.howItWorks: Detection triggers a time delay and alarm, then CO2 is released from high- or low-pressure storage. In total flooding, CO2 is raised to roughly 34% or more of the room's atmosphere — enough to smother the fire and to kill anyone still inside. In local application, nozzles spray CO2 directly onto one hazard, such as a printing press or dip tank, without flooding the whole room. Because of the danger, systems require lockout valves for maintenance, odorizers so a leak is noticed, and warning signage.
guide.market: Installed systems sold through authorized distributors and installers; Firetrace (High Pressure CO2) and KiddeFenwal are among the makers. Because it is lethal at design concentration, it is limited to spaces that are normally unoccupied.

features.label: Total flooding
features.detail: Fills an enclosure to a smothering concentration.

features.label: Local application
features.detail: Targets a single machine or process rather than the whole room.

features.label: Mandatory safeguards
features.detail: Lockout valves, pre-discharge alarms and time delay, odorizers and signage are part of the system, not options.

features.label: No residue
features.detail: Equipment is not coated or soaked.

costs.upfront: USD $4–$8 per sq ft (≈ CAD $5.50–$11); USD $20,000–$100,000+ per project.
costs.consumables: CO2 refill after discharge. No reliable public figure — get quotes.
costs.ancillary: Lockouts, signage, odorizers and alarm integration.
costs.fiveYear: Semiannual cylinder weighing and annual system test. No reliable public figure for service contracts — get quotes.

differentiators.label: Versus inert gas
differentiators.detail: Both lower oxygen, but inert gas systems are designed to leave a survivable atmosphere. CO2 at design concentration is not survivable.

differentiators.label: Versus clean agents
differentiators.detail: Clean agents are designed for occupied rooms; CO2 is not. Choose CO2 only where nobody is normally present.

buying.lead: Weeks for design and installation
buying.where: Not sold to end users — through authorized special-hazard distributors and installers.
buying.note: Ask how the system will be locked out during maintenance and who controls the lockout.

install.time: Days to weeks
install.note: Signage, alarms and lockouts are part of the install and must be complete before the system is armed.

ongoing.note: Semiannual weighing of cylinders and an annual system test. Train everyone who enters the space on the alarm and the lockout procedure.

alternatives.name: Inert gas
alternatives.note: Gas flooding designed to be survivable for short exposure.

alternatives.name: FK-5-1-12 clean agent
alternatives.note: For enclosures where people may be present.

alternatives.name: Water mist
alternatives.note: For machinery enclosures with a listed design.

guide.verdict: Use it only where nobody is normally present, and treat the lockout procedure as seriously as the fire protection. Anywhere people work, choose an agent designed for occupied spaces.

standards.CA: NFPA 12 design; ask for ULC-listed components — ask the distributor for ULC-listed hardware and confirm with the local fire authority.
standards.US: NFPA 12 design, including lockout requirements; systems UL and FM listed.

guide.whoNeeds: Normally unoccupied machinery spaces, vaults and industrial processes, under NFPA 12. Not for occupied spaces.
caveats: Life-safety hazard: total-flooding concentrations are lethal. NFPA 12 requires lockouts, and our cost source explicitly says it is not recommended for occupied spaces.
