name: Aerosol-Can Fire Sprays
brand: First Alert (EZ Fire Spray AF400) · Tundra
pick: An extra at the stove — not a substitute for a listed extinguisher
priceNote: No reliable public price
summary: Spray-can-sized products sold for kitchens and cars that discharge a wet-chemical or water-based agent for roughly 30 seconds. They are easy to use but much smaller than a real extinguisher, and they are not listed and rated the way a portable extinguisher is.
pros: Simple to use: point and press, no pin or hose
Small enough to keep beside the stove or in a car
The First Alert AF400 retail specification cites Class K (cooking oil) and electrical conductivity test methods
cons: Not a listed or rated extinguisher; it does not count toward any code requirement
Only effective on very small, early fires
No pressure gauge and disposable, so you cannot check its charge
bestFor: A grab-it-first extra beside the stove in a home that already has a listed multipurpose extinguisher.

links.label: First Alert AF400 EZ Fire Spray — retailer spec sheet

guide.howItWorks: A pressurised can releases a wet-chemical or water-based agent through a spray nozzle, for roughly 30 seconds. The agent cools the fuel and, on cooking oil, forms a film over the surface. There is no gauge and the can is single-use. The quantity of agent is small, so it can only deal with a fire that is still very small.
guide.market: First Alert / BRK's AF400 EZ Fire Spray is the best-known product; Tundra is the other name in the category. The AF400's retailer specification cites 'UL711A (Class K), UL711 Electrical Conductivity (Class C) up to 35,000 Volts' and a Korean standard, KOFEIS 0108, for Class A. Those are references to test methods; a UL listing or rating was not shown. UL's list of extinguisher standards contains no standard for aerosol-type extinguishers. We found no reliable public price.

features.label: Spray-can format
features.detail: No pin, hose or squeeze handle to learn. That ease is the honest selling point.

features.label: Wet-chemical/water agent
features.detail: Suited to small cooking-oil and ordinary-combustible fires, according to the cited test methods, with far less mess than dry powder.

features.label: Cited test methods, not a listing
features.detail: The AF400 spec references UL 711A and UL 711 test methods and a Korean standard. That is not the same as a UL-listed extinguisher with a rating such as 2-A:10-B:C.

features.label: No gauge
features.detail: You cannot check whether it is still charged; you rely on the expiry date.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure.
costs.consumables: Replace after any use or at expiry.
costs.ancillary: None, but you still need a listed extinguisher alongside it.
costs.fiveYear: No reliable public figure; assume at least one replacement at expiry.

differentiators.label: Versus a listed 2-A:10-B:C extinguisher
differentiators.detail: The listed unit carries far more agent, has a gauge, carries a tested rating and counts toward code requirements. The can does none of those. It is an extra, never the primary.

differentiators.label: Versus a fire blanket or a lid
differentiators.detail: For a pan fire, smothering with a lid or blanket is cheap and reliable. The spray is a convenience alongside that, not a replacement for good cooking habits.

differentiators.label: Versus fire-extinguishing balls
differentiators.detail: The spray at least lets you aim. Throwable balls have no nozzle or controlled discharge, and the CPSC has warned consumers off one brand.

buying.lead: Off the shelf
buying.where: US: Home Depot, Lowe's, Ace Hardware, Amazon and Walmart. Canada: Canadian Tire and Home Depot Canada availability not verified.
buying.note: Buy it in addition to a listed multipurpose extinguisher, not instead of one.

install.time: None
install.note: Keep it within reach of the stove but not above it, where you would have to reach over flames.

ongoing.note: Check the expiry date and replace after any use, even a short burst.

alternatives.name: Listed 2-A:10-B:C (or larger) multipurpose extinguisher
alternatives.note: The primary extinguisher for a home. Buy this first.

alternatives.name: Pan lid or fire blanket
alternatives.note: The simplest way to put out a small stovetop oil fire.

guide.verdict: Fine as an extra at the stove, because it is easy to use in a panic. It is not a listed, rated extinguisher and should not be your only one; put a listed 2-A:10-B:C or larger unit in the kitchen first.

standards.CA: No Canadian listing shown.
standards.US: No UL listing or rating shown. The First Alert AF400 retailer spec cites UL 711A (Class K) and UL 711 electrical conductivity test methods plus Korean standard KOFEIS 0108; UL's extinguisher standards list has no aerosol-type extinguisher standard.

guide.whoNeeds: No one is required to have one, and it is not code-recognised as a substitute for a listed portable extinguisher. Reasonable as a supplementary kitchen or car item.
caveats: Not a listed/rated extinguisher; does not count toward any code requirement.
A listed 2-A:10-B:C or larger unit should be the primary extinguisher.
Effective only on very small, early fires.

name: Throwable Fire-Extinguishing Balls
brand: Elide (now E FIRE USA) · unbranded marketplace sellers
pick: Skip it — not a substitute for a listed extinguisher
priceNote: USD $95–$120 per ball for Elide, per the CPSC
summary: Balls of dry chemical powder that burst when thrown into a fire or engulfed by one. On March 28, 2024 the US Consumer Product Safety Commission warned consumers to immediately stop using Elide-brand balls because they can fail to extinguish fires, with a risk of serious injury or death.
pros: Requires no training to deploy
Can in principle activate unattended if a fire reaches it
No pressure to maintain
cons: CPSC warning (March 28, 2024, updated July 17, 2026): Elide balls can fail to extinguish fires; the company did not agree to a recall
No aiming, nozzle or controlled discharge; performance depends on where it lands
Costs several times as much as a listed multipurpose extinguisher
bestFor: Nobody. Spend the money on a listed multipurpose extinguisher and interconnected alarms.

links.label: CPSC warning on Elide fire-extinguishing balls (March 2024)

guide.howItWorks: A shell holds dry chemical powder around a heat-sensitive fuse. When the ball is thrown into flames, or a fire reaches where it sits, the shell ruptures and scatters the powder. There is no nozzle, no aiming and no control over how long or where the agent is discharged, so the outcome depends on the ball landing in the right spot and the fire being small enough for one burst of powder.
guide.market: Sold online, notably by Elide through elidefireus.com (now E FIRE USA), and through marketplaces. The CPSC put Elide's price at USD $95–$120 per ball, roughly CAD $130–$165 at ~1.38. The CPSC tested Elide balls against UL 299, the standard for dry-chemical extinguishers, and found they lack a pressure gauge or indicator, a locking device, a self-closing valve and a nozzle. It issued its warning on March 28, 2024 and updated it on July 17, 2026; the company did not agree to a recall. We found no Health Canada notice either way.

features.label: Heat-activated burst
features.detail: The ball ruptures when heated. There is no way to direct it once it goes.

features.label: Dry chemical powder
features.detail: The same family of agent as many portable extinguishers, but without any of the hardware that controls discharge.

features.label: What is missing
features.detail: The CPSC found no pressure gauge or indicator, no locking device, no self-closing valve and no nozzle — the features UL 299 expects of a dry-chemical extinguisher.

costs.upfront: USD $95–$120 per ball for Elide, per the CPSC (≈ CAD $130–$165 converted).
costs.consumables: Single-use.
costs.ancillary: None.
costs.fiveYear: The purchase price, which would cover a listed multipurpose extinguisher several times over.

differentiators.label: Versus a listed extinguisher
differentiators.detail: A UL-listed dry-chemical extinguisher has a gauge, a nozzle and a controlled discharge you can aim and stop. The CPSC found the Elide ball has none of these, and that it can fail to put out fires.

differentiators.label: Versus aerosol fire sprays
differentiators.detail: Neither is a listed extinguisher, but a spray can at least be aimed. The ball cannot.

buying.lead: Online only
buying.where: Online direct (Elide, now E FIRE USA, via elidefireus.com) and online marketplaces. We are not linking to sellers.
buying.note: We recommend against buying these. If you already own Elide balls, the CPSC told consumers to stop using them immediately.

install.time: None
install.note: No installation. Do not rely on one mounted near a stove or panel as fire protection.

ongoing.note: Nothing to maintain, and nothing to check: with no gauge you cannot tell whether it is still serviceable.

alternatives.name: Listed 2-A:10-B:C (or larger) multipurpose extinguisher
alternatives.note: Cheaper, aimable and tested. The right tool for a home.

alternatives.name: Interconnected smoke alarms
alternatives.note: Early warning matters more than any extinguisher; most people should get out, not fight the fire.

guide.verdict: Skip it. The CPSC's March 2024 warning says Elide balls can fail to extinguish fires and lack basic extinguisher features, and the company did not agree to a recall. Buy a listed multipurpose extinguisher instead.

standards.CA: No Canadian listing, and no Health Canada action that we could find.
standards.US: No listing. CPSC tested Elide balls against UL 299 and found them lacking a pressure gauge/indicator, locking device, self-closing valve and nozzle; warning issued March 28, 2024, updated July 17, 2026.

guide.whoNeeds: No one. They have no code recognition.
caveats: CPSC warning (March 28, 2024): stop using Elide balls immediately — they can fail to extinguish fires, with risk of serious injury or death.
Elide did not agree to a recall, so units remain in circulation.
Other brands sold on marketplaces work the same way; we found no listed product in the category.

name: Plumis Automist Targeted Water Mist
pick: Interesting, but check with your building department first
priceNote: Installer-quoted; no price published
summary: A wall- or under-cabinet-mounted unit that detects a fire and aims a high-pressure water mist at it from a rotating head, using mains water and a small pump. It is marketed as a lighter alternative to home sprinklers; Canadian availability is not confirmed.
pros: Uses a fraction of the water of a sprinkler
Installs on a standard plumbing connection and electrical supply, without piping every ceiling
Certified under UL 2167A (announced November 11, 2024), with components tested to UL 268
cons: UL 2167A is an outline of investigation, not a full standard; it substitutes for NFPA 13D only if your local authority accepts it
Protects the targeted rooms only, not the whole house
No published price and no confirmed Canadian availability
bestFor: US open-plan kitchens and living areas where a full sprinkler retrofit is impractical and the local building authority will accept it.

guide.howItWorks: Heat and smoke sensors detect and locate the fire. A small pump then drives water from the home's supply through a nozzle on a rotating head that aims at the fire and discharges a fine, high-pressure mist. Fine droplets absorb heat quickly, so it uses a fraction of a sprinkler's water. The unit connects to a standard plumbing point and electrical supply, typically in an open-plan kitchen or living room.
guide.market: Made by Plumis in the UK, where it is mainly used to satisfy fire-safety requirements for open-plan layouts. The US site says it is now available across the US through installers and showrooms; a 2024 announcement named Ferguson Fire & Fabrication as exclusive North American distributor. Canada is not mentioned and we could not confirm it is sold there. No price is published; expect an installer quote.

features.label: Targeted discharge
features.detail: The head aims at the fire rather than wetting the whole room. That is the core of the water-saving claim.

features.label: Mains water plus pump
features.detail: Runs off the domestic supply with an electric pump, so it needs a power supply as well as plumbing.

features.label: UL 2167A certification
features.detail: Announced November 11, 2024 under UL 2167A, the outline of investigation for targeted water mist units in one- and two-family homes, with components tested to UL 268.

features.label: Room-level coverage
features.detail: Each unit protects the space it covers. It is not a whole-house system.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure; Automist does not publish a price.
costs.consumables: No reliable public figure.
costs.ancillary: A plumbing connection and an electrical supply at the mounting point, by the installer.
costs.fiveYear: No reliable public figure. Maintenance is per manufacturer; ask the installer.

differentiators.label: Versus an NFPA 13D sprinkler system
differentiators.detail: 13D is the established, code-recognised residential standard covering the living space. Automist covers targeted rooms and is accepted in place of 13D only where the local authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) agrees; the US site does not claim AHJ approval.

differentiators.label: Versus doing nothing in an open-plan room
differentiators.detail: In the UK it is used to make open-plan layouts acceptable. In North America that argument depends entirely on your building department.

differentiators.label: The listing caveat
differentiators.detail: Being certified to UL 2167A is real, but an outline of investigation is not a full consensus standard. Do not read it as equivalent to a listed sprinkler system.

name: Automatic Stove Shut-Off Devices
pick: Prevention for forgetful cooks — ask for the listing mark
priceNote: Prices not shown on the maker pages we checked
summary: Controllers that cut power or gas to a stove when cooking is left unattended or when a smoke alarm sounds. They prevent fires rather than put them out, and suit seniors, people with dementia and rental units.
pros: Addresses unattended cooking, a leading cause of kitchen fires, before there is a fire
iGuardStove's gas model shuts the gas valve and includes an unburned-gas sensor
FireAvert plugs in between the range and the outlet, with optional monitoring and text alerts
cons: Neither maker's site states a UL, cUL, CSA or ETL listing
Sound-triggered devices only act if the smoke alarm actually detects the fire
Prices and retail availability were not verified
bestFor: Households with an older adult or someone with memory loss, and landlords of rental or assisted-living units.

guide.howItWorks: Two approaches. iGuardStove uses a motion sensor to tell whether anyone is in the kitchen; if the stove is on and nobody has been seen for a set time, it cuts power, and its gas model closes a gas valve and adds a sensor for unburned gas. FireAvert sits between the range plug and the outlet and listens for the specific sound pattern of a smoke alarm; when it hears one, it cuts power to the range, and can send text alerts through optional monitoring. Neither puts out a fire that has already started; they remove the heat source.
guide.market: iGuardFire, maker of iGuardStove, is based in Kelowna, BC; its site shows a 2026 model as pre-sale. FireAvert is a Utah company whose storefront displays CAD prices to Canadian visitors. Neither page we fetched showed prices, and neither states a safety listing. Separately, since April 4, 2019, UL 858 has required new electric coil cooktops to pass an abnormal-operation cooking-oil ignition test, so newer coil ranges include built-in temperature limiting.

features.label: Motion-based timer (iGuardStove)
features.detail: Shuts the stove off when the kitchen has been empty too long. Works before any smoke is produced.

features.label: Gas shut-off and gas sensor (iGuardStove gas model)
features.detail: Closes the gas valve and watches for unburned gas, which addresses a burner left on without a flame.

features.label: Alarm-triggered cut-off (FireAvert)
features.detail: Cuts power when it hears the smoke alarm. Simple, but it can only act once the alarm has detected smoke.

features.label: Monitoring and alerts (FireAvert, optional)
features.detail: Text alerts to a family member or caregiver when it trips.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure; prices were not shown on the maker pages we fetched.
costs.consumables: None stated.
costs.ancillary: Hardwired or gas installations may need an electrician or gas fitter. No reliable public figure. FireAvert's monitoring is optional and its cost was not shown.
costs.fiveYear: No reliable public figure.

differentiators.label: Prevent versus extinguish
differentiators.detail: These stop unattended cooking from becoming a fire. An extinguisher or lid deals with a fire already burning. They are complements.

differentiators.label: Motion versus sound
differentiators.detail: Motion-based shut-off works earlier, before smoke. Sound-based shut-off depends on a working smoke alarm close enough to the stove to detect the fire.

differentiators.label: Versus a newer coil range
differentiators.detail: Coil ranges built to UL 858 since April 2019 include temperature limiting that targets cooking-oil ignition. That covers one fire mode on one type of stove; it does not cover gas or older ranges.

buying.lead: Direct order; iGuardStove's 2026 model was shown as pre-sale
buying.where: Direct from the manufacturers' websites (iguardfire.com, fireavert.com). Retail availability at Amazon or Best Buy was not verified.
buying.note: Before buying, ask the maker which certification mark (UL, cUL, CSA or ETL) the specific model carries.

install.time: Minutes for a plug-in unit; an electrician or gas fitter for hardwired and gas models
tools: Electrician or gas fitter for hardwired/gas
install.note: For a sound-triggered unit, make sure a working smoke alarm is close enough to the kitchen to hear a stovetop fire early.

ongoing.note: Per manufacturer. Test the shut-off periodically and keep the smoke alarm it depends on tested and in service.

alternatives.name: A newer electric coil range built to UL 858 (since April 2019)
alternatives.note: Has built-in temperature limiting aimed at cooking-oil ignition.

alternatives.name: Interconnected smoke alarms plus a listed extinguisher and pan lid
alternatives.note: The baseline kitchen setup every home should have regardless.

guide.verdict: A sensible prevention device where unattended cooking is a real risk, such as an older relative living alone or a rental unit. Neither maker states a safety listing on its site, so ask for the certification mark on the exact model before you buy.

name: Lithium-Ion and E-Bike Charging Safety at Home
pick: Buy certified, charge in the right place — skip the gadgets
priceNote: Mostly habits; no product to price
summary: E-bikes, scooters and power-tool batteries can produce intense, fast-spreading fires, especially when the battery or charger is uncertified or damaged. The main protection is buying certified products and charging them safely, not a special accessory.
pros: The most effective steps (certified products, original charger, sensible charging location) cost little or nothing
Addresses the cause rather than trying to contain a battery fire after it starts
A smoke or heat alarm near the charging spot gives early warning cheaply
cons: No product makes an uncertified or damaged battery safe
'Fireproof' charging bags sold online are generally unlisted, and their effectiveness for large e-bike packs is doubtful
bestFor: Any household that charges an e-bike, e-scooter or large power-tool battery indoors.

guide.howItWorks: A damaged, defective or badly charged lithium-ion cell can go into thermal runaway: it heats itself, vents flammable gas and ignites neighbouring cells, producing a fire that is intense, fast and hard to put out. Certification standards test the whole electrical system, battery and charger together, to reduce that risk. Safe practice then limits the consequences: charge with the manufacturer's charger, on a hard surface, not overnight and not where a fire would block your way out, with an alarm nearby, and retire any battery that is damaged or swollen.
guide.market: There is no single product here. The protection comes from buying e-bikes and scooters certified to UL 2849 or UL 2272 from mainstream retailers, and from charging habits. Storage cabinets and charging bags are sold, but they reduce rather than eliminate risk, and the bags commonly sold online are generally unlisted. New York City requires e-bikes and batteries sold there to be certified to UL 2849 or UL 2271.

features.label: Certified e-bikes and scooters
features.detail: Look for UL 2849 (e-bike electrical systems) or UL 2272 (personal e-mobility devices) on the product, not just on the charger.

features.label: Use the original charger
features.detail: A mismatched charger is a common route to overcharging. Replace a lost charger with the manufacturer's part.

features.label: Charge where a fire cannot trap you
features.detail: Not overnight, not in a hallway or by the only exit, and on a hard surface away from soft furnishings.

features.label: Alarm coverage
features.detail: A smoke or heat alarm near the charging spot, ideally interconnected, so a battery fire is heard throughout the house.

features.label: Retire damaged packs
features.detail: Swollen, dented, wet or overheating batteries should be taken out of service and recycled, not charged.

costs.upfront: No product cost for the practices themselves. Certified e-bikes and replacement batteries vary widely; no reliable public figure.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: A smoke or heat alarm for the charging area if it is not already covered.
costs.fiveYear: No reliable public figure.

differentiators.label: Certification versus accessories
differentiators.detail: A certified battery and charger addresses the cause. A bag or cabinet only tries to contain a fire after it starts.

differentiators.label: Charging bags
differentiators.detail: 'Fireproof' LiPo bags sold online are generally unlisted, and their usefulness for a large e-bike pack is doubtful. Do not treat one as permission to charge an uncertified battery indoors.

buying.lead: Not applicable
buying.where: Certified e-bikes, scooters and batteries from mainstream retailers. There is no specific product to buy for this entry.
buying.note: Check the certification on the product itself, and buy replacement batteries and chargers from the original manufacturer.

install.time: Minutes to choose and set up a charging spot
install.note: Pick a charging location on a hard surface, away from exits and bedrooms, with an alarm nearby.

ongoing.note: Inspect batteries regularly, replace damaged packs and recycle old ones properly rather than putting them in household waste.

alternatives.name: Heat or smoke alarm at the charging spot
alternatives.note: Cheap early warning, especially for a garage or basement charging area.

alternatives.name: Charging outdoors or in a detached space
alternatives.note: Keeps a battery fire away from the people in the house.

guide.verdict: Buy certified e-bikes and scooters, use the original charger, and charge where a fire would not trap anyone. That does more than any accessory. Treat charging bags as a weak extra, not a solution.

standards.CA: No Canada-specific standard; look for products certified to the same UL standards.
standards.US: UL 2849 (e-bike electrical systems), UL 2272 (personal e-mobility devices) and UL 2271 (batteries).

guide.whoNeeds: Everyone who charges an e-bike, e-scooter or large battery at home. New York City requires e-bikes and batteries sold there to be certified to UL 2849 or UL 2271.
caveats: 'Fireproof' LiPo charging bags sold online are generally unlisted; effectiveness for large e-bike packs is doubtful.
Local rules on e-bike sales and charging are changing quickly; check your city's current rules.

name: Home Battery Storage (ESS) Fire Safety
pick: Use a listed system and a licensed installer
priceNote: Installed system; no reliable public figure
summary: Wall-mounted home batteries, often paired with solar for backup power, carry rules on where they go, how much capacity is allowed and what detection is needed, all to manage the risk of thermal runaway. The protection comes from a listed system installed by a licensed electrician or solar installer to code.
pros: Code rules on siting, capacity and separation manage the main risk
Listed systems have been tested as a whole, not just cell by cell
Installation by a licensed installer brings permitting and inspection
cons: A battery fire is hard to put out, so siting rules matter more than suppression
Confirm the code sections with your installer and local authority
bestFor: Homeowners adding solar backup or whole-home battery storage who want to know what a compliant installation looks like.

guide.howItWorks: The risk is thermal runaway: a failing cell heats itself, vents flammable gas and spreads to neighbouring cells. Codes manage this by limiting where batteries go in a dwelling and how much capacity is allowed, requiring listed systems, separating the batteries from living spaces, and often requiring a smoke or heat alarm in the room where they are installed. The system itself is listed as a whole, and its fire behaviour is characterised by a standard test method.
guide.market: Home batteries are installed by licensed electricians and solar installers rather than bought off the shelf. Prices depend on capacity and the installation, so get quotes; insist on a system listed to UL 9540 (CSA C22.2 No. 340 in Canada).

features.label: Listed system
features.detail: In the US, look for a system listed to UL 9540; in Canada, CSA C22.2 No. 340. Ask the installer for the listing.

features.label: Fire test data
features.detail: UL 9540A is a test method that characterises how a battery fire propagates. It informs siting and separation requirements.

features.label: Siting and separation
features.detail: Codes restrict where in a home a battery may go and require separation from living spaces. A garage or exterior wall is common; a bedroom closet is not.

features.label: Detection
features.detail: A smoke or heat alarm in the installation room is often required. Interconnect it with the rest of the house.

costs.upfront: No reliable public figure.
costs.consumables: None.
costs.ancillary: Permits, any required alarm in the installation room, and any separation work. No reliable public figure.
costs.fiveYear: No reliable public figure. Maintenance is per manufacturer, including firmware updates.

differentiators.label: Listed system versus assembled components
differentiators.detail: A system listed as a whole has been tested together. A do-it-yourself assembly of cells, inverter and enclosure has not.

differentiators.label: Siting versus suppression
differentiators.detail: There is no practical home extinguisher answer to a large battery fire. Where the battery is placed, and how it is separated from where people sleep, is the safety measure.

buying.lead: Design, permitting and inspection through the installer
buying.where: Licensed solar installers and electrical contractors. Not an off-the-shelf retail purchase.
buying.note: Ask the installer which listing the system carries, where it will be sited and why, and whether a smoke or heat alarm will be added in that room.

install.time: No reliable public figure; depends on the system and permitting
install.note: Installation must follow the electrical code and local fire rules. Not a do-it-yourself job.

ongoing.note: Follow the manufacturer's maintenance schedule and keep firmware updated. Test the alarm in the installation room with the rest of the house.

alternatives.name: Portable generator
alternatives.note: A different risk profile (carbon monoxide and fuel) but no lithium storage in the house.

alternatives.name: Grid-tied solar without storage
alternatives.note: No battery, no thermal-runaway risk, but no backup when the grid is down.

guide.verdict: A home battery can be installed safely, but the safety comes from a listed system, correct siting and a licensed installer, not from anything you add afterward. Confirm the listing and siting with your installer before you sign.

standards.CA: CSA C22.2 No. 340 for the system; Canadian Electrical Code and provincial rules for installation.
standards.US: UL 9540 (system listing) and UL 9540A (fire test method); NFPA 855, IRC R328 and the IFC govern installation.

guide.whoNeeds: Anyone installing battery storage in a dwelling. In the US, NFPA 855, IRC R328 and the IFC apply; in Canada, the Canadian Electrical Code and provincial rules.
caveats: Code requirements differ by province, state, city and code edition. Confirm with your authority having jurisdiction (the local fire official or building department) before relying on a specific clause.
Prices depend on capacity, the inverter and the installation; get at least two quotes from licensed installers.
guide.costNote: Retail prices from public listings, October 2026; CAD where Canadian listings exist, otherwise converted at ~1.38.
